Levara seized the line. The marker pulled one way, the current another. "It will foul the steering oar."

"Not if you let it run."

The rocks to leeward were not close enough to kill them, only close enough to tear away a plank and make the rest of the night intolerable. She could retie the line and call Holdfast, but Farwake was already beneath them. The two powers would meet in the hull.

"Levara." Ambel dropped the sail and set the steering oar hard. "Give me the bow."

She opened her hand.

The line hissed over the gunwale. Freed of her pull, the bight slackened around the marker. Ambel used the last of the outward current to bring the bow across it, precise as a needle passing through cloth.

"Now."

Levara leaned out with the boat hook, caught the bight, and lifted. Salt scraped stone. For a moment the line hung heavy enough to drag her shoulder down; then Ambel shifted his weight without being asked, the boat rose under her, and the loop came free.

They drifted clear in ordinary tide. The line lay in a sodden heap between them. Levara's coat clung from hip to ankle, and one of Ambel's sleeves had filled with water.

He peeled it back and wrung it out. "A persuasive demonstration."

"Of what?"

"You let Holdfast catch me and promise you'll loosen the line afterward."

"I did not foul it deliberately."

"I know."

"Then don't use an accident as a doctrinal argument."

"You began interviewing my soul before we cleared the breakwater."

There it was: not anger, yet, but the withdrawal of an ease she had come to depend on without ever naming it. He stepped around her to raise the sail. Usually he warned her before the boom crossed. This time she had to duck.

Beyond the mouth, Brackwater Reach widened beneath rain clouds thinning from charcoal to pewter. The reef made a black half-circle around it, marked by three lanterns and the pale churn of Farwake's water. Ambel set their course for the first light. Levara flaked the wet home line into exact coils and tried to find a version of the truth that would not sound like surrender.

She found twelve inadequate ones before the first reef bell.

The bell hung from an arch driven into the rock. Ambel brought them alongside, and Levara passed the line through its ring. The instant her knot took, the chop flattened. The sail sagged.

Fresh crystals lifted on the rope beneath her fingers.

PRESS THE COST OF ALWAYS LEAVING. OFFER HIM SAFE HARBOR.

Ambel was close enough to read over her shoulder.

For seven years she had watched him find laughter in council deadlocks, funerals delayed by contrary winds, fish guts on ceremonial hems. Now his face emptied.

"There," he said. "That saves time."

Levara dragged the rope through the water. The letters dissolved, but he had seen them.

"Farwake spoke to me at the launch," Ambel continued. He sat on the opposite bench and pulled the wet sleeve straight over his wrist. "Through the channel under the cradle. 'Bring her beyond every fastening.' He promised a clean outward current for every ship I bless this season if I succeeded."

The reef bell moved once above them, though Holdfast had stilled the water. Its note was small and sour.

"Holdfast offered no inducement," Levara said.

"That sounds like him."

"You are not entitled to mock—"

"I am wet to the skin because your holy rope tried to stay behind. Allow me one remark."

She pressed both hands to the coil. "He commanded me to bring you home. I was not told what means were permitted, but conversion obtained under false pretenses would be invalid under the third covenant, and any benefit offered to you would have to be disclosed before assent."

Ambel looked toward the lantern, not at her. "You worked out the proper way to recruit me."

"I worked out what would not count."

"That isn't better."

"It is materially different."

"To you."

The answer struck because it was careless. Levara stood so quickly the boat rocked inside Holdfast's calm.

"Yes, to me. I am not a trap my god sets. I had the command, and I questioned it. I asked you questions rather than lying. Poor questions, apparently, but mine."

"Were they?"

"Some of them."

At last he looked at her.

Levara's fluency deserted her at precisely the point it was supposed to prove useful. Rain ticked on the slack sail. The lantern above them put a stripe of amber along Ambel's cheek and made the rest of him difficult to read.

"I have considered," she began, "whether a change of allegiance would remove certain conflicts that neither office can otherwise accommodate."

"Stop making a clause."

"It helps me not lie."

"Then make it shorter."

She sat. The bread had gone to paste in her mouth. "I thought if you came to Holdfast, I would be permitted to want you."

Ambel's hand tightened on the tiller. "Permitted by whom?"

"Everyone."

"That's a lot of people to fit in this boat."

"You know what I mean."

"I do. That's why I'm angry."

He pulled the line free. Holdfast's calm broke at once, and the bell began to swing in the returning chop. Ambel did not call Farwake. For a few breaths they rose and fell in water claimed by neither god, the sail hanging empty above them.

"I won't be captured ground," he said. The anecdotes and jokes were gone. "Not for Farwake. Not for you."

"I don't want a trophy."

"You want the difficulty removed."

"Of course I do."

He flinched.

"No, listen. I want to speak to you on a morning that isn't prescribed by treaty. I want to disagree with you without sixty people recording which of us blinked. I have wanted that for years. I imagined one means of obtaining it, and that means was wrong. Those statements are not equivalent."

"You always do that."

"Distinguish things?"

"Answer the implication and leave the person waiting."

Levara took her hands off the rope. "You heard that I was willing to erase you."

His jaw shifted. After a moment, he nodded.

"I wasn't," she said. "I was willing to imagine you choosing what I chose. That is not harmless, but it is not erasure."

"No. It isn't."

He had done what he always demanded of disputants and rarely managed when the dispute touched him: corrected himself while the correction still cost something.

Levara waited. The reef bell knocked twice. Farther out, a line of foam marched past the lantern toward open water.

"I imagined it too," Ambel said.

For one beat, she heard nothing but the reef bell.

"The first three years. Maybe four. Farwake would have liked the harbor to see you walk down his launch steps. I thought you might breathe easier if every promise didn't need a knot around it."

"You mistook devotion for fear."

"Yes."

"Holdfast stilled the surge against the south quay when the piles split. He gives the ferry families sleep in winter. His shrine takes in people whose own houses have turned them out. I do not love him because I have failed to imagine leaving."

"All right."

"That is not an answer."

"It is. You are staying because you mean it. I heard you."

The simple sentence left her with nowhere to press. Ambel looked tired now, and cold. His hand shook once as he reached for the halyard.

"Farwake has carried people away from lives that were killing them," he said. "Some came back. Some didn't. He doesn't call every departure a wound. I mean that too."

Levara could have named the families for whom a departure had been exactly that. The argument was seven years old and would survive them both.

"I hear you," she said.

Ambel raised the sail and called Farwake. The current gathered beneath them, not gently, but cleanly. They rounded the lantern and entered the long dark arc of the reef.

They worked the next two stations with little speech. At one, Levara's chilled fingers failed to pull a salt-crusted knot snug, and Ambel held the lantern while she worked it loose with her teeth. At the next, his bread wrapping escaped. She hooked it before it went overboard and tucked it under his thigh without comment.

The tide fell. Black shelves of reef emerged, shining with weed. Behind them, the harbor lights drew closer together; from this distance Levara could not tell which lamps burned at whose shrine.

Ambel broke the silence. "What happens if neither of us converts?"

Levara had been preparing an answer for half the circuit. "The divine commands fail. We complete the truce. We report that no change of allegiance occurred. Any further disclosure would require consideration of our duties to our offices, our councils, and the people affected."

"That answer has furniture."

"You asked what happens."

"I asked what happens to us."

She watched the lantern light pass over his hands, broad-palmed and nicked by years of rope. Once she had thought attraction should feel like disorder. This did not. It felt like recognizing a route from the water after knowing it only from charts: every turn already present, the whole shape newly unavoidable.

"I love you," she said. "I will not ask you to leave Farwake for it."

Ambel missed the next stroke. The steering oar bumped the hull.

Levara had given testimony before hostile councils, families waiting for news, and the god whose water went still when displeased. Nothing had exposed her like Ambel staring at the oar as if it had betrayed him.

"You needn't answer in the same form," she said.

"Please be quiet."

She obeyed.

He steered them past the reef's last tooth. Open water pulled at the hull. The Farwake shrine's distant pennants streamed seaward, all pointing away from Brackwater Reach.

"I brought the honey loaf because you don't eat when you're trying to defeat me," he said at last. "I keep your amendment copies in a dry box. I know which floorboard outside your council room squeaks because I stand there before meetings and decide whether to go in early." He rubbed both hands over his face. "I don't know how to say it without making it sound like evidence."

"It is persuasive evidence."

"Levara."

"Sorry."

"I love you too. I don't know what we do now."

"Neither do I."

That startled another laugh out of him. This one broke in the middle.

On the return to the harbor mouth, they settled only one thing. Six days after the circuit, before the noon bell, they would meet at the baker's back table above the rope market. Ambel rejected Levara's first proposed hour because it coincided with his blessing of a westbound grain ship. Levara rejected his because the bakery closed then. They would wear ordinary coats over their vestments and each pay for their own meal.

"Why that last condition?" Ambel asked.

"So neither god can call it tribute."

"Or we could split the bill because we're adults."

"That is what I said."

"It absolutely wasn't."

The harbor mouth lay ahead. Here the gods' powers crossed, and the circuit required a final, exact exchange. Ambel lowered the sail but did not yet dismiss Farwake's current. Levara held the home line ready but untied.

Between the two acts, they coasted through the dark on momentum alone.

Ambel touched two fingers to her cheek. "May I?"

"Yes."

The kiss was cold, brief, and awkward around the raised collar of Levara's coat. The boat turned half a degree while neither of them attended to it. Then Ambel sat back, cleared his throat, and took up the steering oar.

"We're east of the marker," he said.

"I noticed."

"You did not."

"Correct the heading."

He did. At the boundary ring, he lifted the oar from the water.

"Farwake," he called, and his ceremonial voice carried toward the open reef, "what goes out belongs first to itself."

The outward current released the keel.

Levara caught the iron ring, passed the home line through it, and tied six turns. Salt whitened the fibers beneath her hands.

"Holdfast," she answered, "what goes out remains answerable to home."

The harbor water stilled around them. Their old disagreement stood intact.

Together, as the truce required, they said, "Between the claims, let passage stand."

The knot tightened. Farwake's last swell spent itself against Holdfast's calm without rocking the boat. Neither god sent another word. Levara untied, and they rowed the remaining inner water from ring to ring.

Dawn had thinned the sky when the waiting crews reached for the circuit boat. The Farwake launch keeper took the bow on the seaward side. Holdfast's keeper caught Levara's stern line and called, "Easy. Two turns."

Levara made two turns around the quay post. The water went smooth beneath her palm.

Across the narrow channel, Ambel stepped onto his own wharf with the wet loaf wrapping tucked firmly under his arm. He did not look back until the crews had begun hauling the boat onto its cradle.

He held up six fingers.

Levara checked the knot once, because it was her work, and went to answer her god.

stories.title: Terms at Four
stories.prompt: You're attending a tea party thrown by a very cute girl. Delicious tea, cake, cookies, and a pie. Then she gets a call from the Prime Minister saying the government will meet her demands if she disarms the satellite and releases the hostages.
stories.body:
# Terms at Four

At four precisely, she opened the door with a tea towel over one shoulder and said, “You’re early.”

Your watch said four precisely too, but arguing about clocks had once consumed eleven minutes of a design review, so you stepped inside.

“I brought nothing,” you said.

“That was the instruction.” She took your coat. “Shoes may stay on. The kitchen tile is cold.”

At thirty-four, your former colleague had made herself cute with the same deliberation she once brought to fault trees: a soft green cardigan, a silver barrette shaped like two leaves, and round spectacles that kept slipping a little down her nose. Nothing about her suggested a child. She was a grown woman with a mortgage, a doctorate, and, until seven months ago, senior authority over an orbital defense platform. The effect was charming. It was also, because you knew her, a warning that she had planned the afternoon down to the teaspoons.

The table confirmed it. A white pot wore a quilted cozy. Beside it waited a smaller pot of jasmine green tea, a squat pot of smoked tea, a three-layer cake glazed pale pink, two plates of cookies, and a deep pie dish under a folded cloth. The room smelled of butter, baked apples, and warm dust from an overworked electronics rack.

“You made too much.”

“You always say that before eating enough for three.”

“I said it once.”

“At the winter calibration.” She indicated your old chair, facing the window. “Black tea first?”

That was how she had taken minutes in the control room: not *tea?* but *black tea first?*, as if the only uncertainty concerned sequence. You sat. Between the sugar bowl and a vase of small white flowers, a pane of dark glass showed a blue curve, three lines of figures, and a pulsing amber square.

You did not touch the cup she poured.

“Is that live?”

She settled opposite you. “Have a cookie.”

“Is it live?”

“Yes.”

The amber square pulsed at the old command cadence. Five seconds lit, two seconds dark. You had watched it through tests, budget hearings, and the all-night argument that ended with your resignation. The figures beside it reported an armed control lattice in orbit and a valid targeting key.

She nudged the nearer plate toward you. The cookies were little rounds, their edges browned evenly, each pressed with the back of a fork.

“Those are the salt ones,” she said. “The sugared ones are by your elbow.”

“You armed it.”

“They armed it. I retained the session.”

“That distinction won’t help anyone under it.”

For the first time she missed a serving cue. The milk jug remained in her hand after your cup was the right color.

“Six members of the security detail are in the lower training suite at the operations annex,” she said. “The locks answer to the same session. They have water, ventilation, and a toilet. No one has been injured.”

The tea touched your tongue before you understood you had picked it up. Hot, strong, exactly enough milk. You put it down.

“Show me.”

She woke a second pane. A wide room appeared under flat ceiling lights. Six adults sat or paced within its white boundary lines. Two wore jackets over formal clothes; four wore the dark uniform of state security. No restraints. One person struck the sealed door with the heel of a hand, stopped, and looked directly into the ceiling camera.

The absurdity did not soften anything. Your old colleague had baked a cake and taken six hostages. Above weather and traffic, a machine the two of you had helped design held an armed key.

“Live challenge,” you said.

She pushed the pane across the table.

You opened the verifier and chose a random phrase from its list. “Ask the person nearest the camera to repeat *violet cup, nineteen*, then hold up both hands.”

She pressed the intercom. Her hosting voice disappeared. “For verification: nearest the camera, repeat violet cup, nineteen. Both hands visible.”

The nearest captive stared upward. “Violet cup, nineteen.” Both hands rose. “Now let us out.”

There was no elegance in the reply, only anger and a dry throat.

“Confirmed,” you said. “Why them?”

“They came to take the maintenance crew.”

“They came under orders.”

“So did the maintenance crew.” She folded the tea towel once and laid it beside her plate. “The crew refused the final arming sequence. They were detained without counsel. The written orders were removed from the case record this morning.”

“And you thought kidnapping would clarify procedure.”

“I thought leverage might.”

On the feed, one of the uniformed captives sat down too quickly. An older person beside them knelt, listened, then looked at the camera.

“Intercom,” you said.

“We have a schedule.”

“Intercom.”

She pressed it.

“What do you need?” you asked.

The kneeling captive answered. “Their cardiac tablets. Jacket pocket, outside this room. They missed the last dose.”

You looked across the cake at your former colleague.

She had already turned to another control. “The corridor cart can bring the jacket to the transfer drawer.”

“Open the drawer before it arrives.”

“That leaves an access path.”

“For a jacket.”

“For anything that fits behind it.” Her eyes moved over three status marks. “I’m checking the outer corridor.”

“They don’t owe you patience.”

Her mouth tightened. At work, pressure had made her more grammatical, never louder. “Outer corridor clear. Transfer drawer opening.”

On the screen, a narrow panel clicked ajar near the floor. Ninety seconds later, a small service cart rolled into view outside the inner window and tipped a dark jacket forward. The kneeling captive pulled it through, found a packet, and passed over two tablets with a paper cup of water. The sick person swallowed.

“Anything else?” you asked through the intercom.

“The door,” the captive said.

You closed the channel before your former colleague could answer.

She poured herself smoked tea. Her hand was steady again. “The government delivers all five maintenance workers to independent counsel, in view of the south camera. The detention record and the original arming orders are filed with the high court. I destroy the targeting key and eject the armed lattice. Then I release the locks.”

“And if they don’t?”

“I keep control.”

“Of a weapon.”

“Of their weapon.”

You reached for a salt cookie because your stomach had mistaken dread for emptiness. It broke cleanly, scattering crumbs onto a tablecloth embroidered with strawberries.

“No,” you said. “You don’t get to hand the noun back to them. You have it.”

She watched you brush the crumbs into your palm. “You still do that.”

“What?”

“Clean the table while telling someone their system is morally indefensible.”

“It used to be your table too.”

That landed. She looked toward the amber pulse.

You had left the platform project when its defensive mandate became a drafting convenience, a phrase broad enough to cover anything the cabinet wanted after midnight. She had stayed, saying somebody had to protect the safe-mode architecture from the inside. For seven months you had wondered whether that had been courage, vanity, or simply her inability to leave a machine unfinished. Now the machine was finished. Now this.

“Give me the full telemetry,” you said.

“After cake.”

“Now.”

“You won’t think better hungry.”

She stood and lifted the cake knife. You nearly shouted at her. Then the display chimed with a government handshake request, and the knife paused above the pink glaze.

“Not yet,” she said. “That’s the liaison channel. The Prime Minister’s office has another seven minutes.”

“You scheduled the head of government between cake and pie?”

“I estimated response times.”

“Of course you did.”

She cut two narrow slices, placing yours on the plate with the painted bird because that had been yours in the control room cupboard. The cake was vanilla and lemon, its layers straight as ruled lines. You hated that it was excellent.

While she ate three careful bites, you opened the telemetry tree. She had granted you read-only access but left the branches uncollapsed. The armed lattice showed one active path. You checked the time stamps against two ground beacons and a civilian tracking clock. No loop. You challenged the orbital unit; its return arrived with the correct light-delay wobble. You searched for shadow keys and dormant targeting branches, then checked the safe-mode design you had written years ago and she had later hardened.

“You kept the dual break,” you said.

“I told you I would.”

“You told me many things in that room.”

She put down her fork. “The burn fuse destroys the key store. The lattice ejects as a cold module. Ground control can’t rebuild either before retrieval, and retrieval takes months.”

“If the ejector fires.”

“We test it every orbit.”

“You test a signal. Show me the physical interlock.”

She opened the hardware channel without argument. That was worse than confidence; it was an old concession, the kind she made only when she wanted you to notice she had prepared for your objection. The pressure seal reported intact. The ejector capacitors were charged. Two independent observers had access to the same public-safe telemetry you did.

There remained an ugly twelve-second interval in which a blackout could resemble an abort. You marked it.

“Who else can stop safe mode?” you asked.

“No one once I commit.”

“Before commit.”

“Me. Ground control can request delay but not cancel.”

“And the hostages?”

“One command opens every inner door. The recovery teams are waiting beyond the outer line.”

“Waiting under whose authority?”

“The Prime Minister’s.”

“Then the government knows where they are.”

“It has for twenty-two minutes.”

You looked at the six people on the feed. One was helping the medicated captive sit upright. Another had taken off a jacket and folded it into a cushion. They knew rescue was close enough to imagine and too far away to trust.

The encrypted phone rang at four forty-three. Its plain double trill was the same sound the old control room phones had made for cafeteria calls.

Your former colleague wiped cake crumbs from her fingertips and answered on speaker. “Good afternoon, Prime Minister.”

The voice that came through was lower than broadcasts made it, roughened by distance or fatigue. “Is your witness present?”

“I’m here,” you said.

“Have you confirmed the six?”

“Live feed and challenge confirmed. One needed medication. They have it now. They are still confined.”

A pause. Faintly, on the far end, paper moved and someone whispered too far from the microphone to make out.

“Have you confirmed control of the platform?” the Prime Minister asked.

“Yes. Armed state is real. So is the proposed safe mode, subject to execution.”

“Thank you.” Then, to your host: “The government will meet your demands if you disarm the satellite and release all six hostages.”

Your former colleague adjusted the pie cloth though it was already centered. “That repeats your message from twenty minutes ago. It does not establish sequence.”

“Release them first.”

“No.” She drew the smoked tea closer without drinking.

“Then begin disarmament.”

“The crew first reaches counsel. The filings must be accepted by the court registry.”

“You are not setting court procedure from a dining room.”

“I am naming the observable conditions.”

“And I am responsible for six people in a locked room and everyone beneath that satellite.” The Prime Minister stopped. When the voice returned, the clauses were shorter. “The crew is in transit. Counsel is waiting. The filing is queued. You will destroy the key when the vehicle crosses the outer gate. You will open the inner doors when the registry returns its receipt. The lattice ejects while my medical team takes custody.”

Your former colleague reached for her pen. “No. Custody can be staged—”

“Stop,” you said.

She did not look at you. “I am trying to prevent substitution.”

“You’re not listening. That sequence makes the hostages wait on a court server.”

The Prime Minister said, “Agreed.”

She aligned the pen with her spoon. “Then offer a dependency that can be verified.”

“Vehicle crosses the gate,” the Prime Minister said. “You commit safe mode. Your witness confirms key destruction. We open the court submission to public receipt. You release the doors. My team crosses the outer line as the lattice ejects. Counsel keeps the crew. No one is returned to detention tonight.”

“The filing includes the signed arming orders and the detention authorization.”

“It includes the complete documents your counsel identified.”

“Not summaries.”

“Complete documents.”

Your former colleague pressed her lips together. Her practiced precision was fraying in a peculiar direction: more conditions, more nouns, less ability to hear when an answer had arrived.

“And the government states on this record that it has met the demands before I open the doors,” she said.

“After the crew reaches counsel and the registry accepts the filing, I will state it.”

“The key goes first,” you said to her. “Not the people.”

She looked at you then. “If they take the crew back—”

“I know why you called me.”

“Do you?”

“You wanted someone who could prove you kept your terms.”

Her gaze dropped to the bird on your cake plate. One untouched corner of the slice remained.

“I wanted someone who would notice if they kept theirs,” she said.

It was the old division of labor, offered across porcelain: she held the line inside; you made the line visible from outside. You had once trusted it. You did not now.

“I’ll notice,” you said. “I won’t call this necessary.”

The encrypted line hissed softly.

“Prime Minister?” she asked.

“Proceed on the sequence your witness described,” came the answer. “My office will remain connected.”

At four fifty-one, she lifted the cloth from the pie. Steam brought up apples, brown sugar, and a sharp scent of citrus peel. She cut it while four screens arranged themselves among the dishes: the south gate, the court receipt, the satellite telemetry, the training suite.

“Cream?” she asked.

You stared at her.

“It is getting warm.”

“No cream.”

“You used to take cream.”

“I stopped.”

She set the jug beside her own plate. She did not ask when.

The pie crust cracked under your fork. On the gate feed, a dark vehicle rolled to a stop. Five people emerged one by one, tired adults in maintenance gray, each carrying nothing. A lawyer waited beyond a painted line with two assistants and an open case. The crew crossed. One stumbled; the others slowed until all five stood on the same side beside counsel.

“Count confirmed,” you said. “Five with counsel.”

“Government confirms transfer,” the Prime Minister said.

Your former colleague entered her command. The amber pulse changed to a red ring.

“Safe mode staged,” she said.

“That isn’t commit.” Your interruption came too loud in the small kitchen.

Her fingers hovered. “I am waiting for the registry.”

“The agreed sequence was commit at the gate.”

“The submission is moving.”

“You asked me to witness terms. Those are the terms.”

For three seconds she kept her hand above the glass. At work, that pause had meant she had found a failure path. Now the timer continued and her hand stayed still.

Then she pressed her thumb to the red ring.

“Commit accepted,” the platform reported in a mild synthetic voice.

The amber pulse vanished. A white bar advanced across the pane.

“Ground control requests hold,” the Prime Minister said.

Your former colleague’s head snapped toward the phone.

“Can they stop it?”

“No,” you said. “Not after commit.”

“Confirm that.”

“The command is irreversible. Hold is only a request to the monitor now.”

The court screen refreshed. A receipt number appeared, followed by a file index. You opened two random pages. Signatures, dates, the arming language you remembered objecting to, and the authorization used to detain the crew. The originals carried registry seals.

“Filing accepted,” you said. “Documents present.”

The Prime Minister drew an audible breath. “The maintenance crew is with independent counsel. The complete documents are filed with the high court. The government has met your demands.”

Your former colleague did not answer immediately. Formal courtesy had left her; perhaps there was no room for it beside the twelve-second gap approaching on the telemetry.

“Release,” you said.

She pressed the lock control.

On the training-suite feed, all six inner-door indicators went green. The door slid aside. For half a second no one moved. Then the captive who had demanded release stepped into the corridor with both empty hands raised. The others followed: two, three, the person who had needed medication supported at one elbow, five, six. A medical team crossed the outer line carrying bags and a folding chair.

“Keep the wide view,” you said.

Your former colleague switched cameras before the nearest official could request it. The freed captives did not thank her. One shouted toward the ceiling; the words blurred under the alarm from the open doors. Another waved the medical team toward the sick person. All six passed the painted outer line. Two medics took the unsteady captive into the chair, checked a wrist monitor, and began talking to them. Four security officers counted aloud and counted again.

“Six released and with the medical team,” you said.

“Confirmed,” the Prime Minister said.

The satellite pane went black.

Your former colleague gripped the edge of the table. “That is early.”

You counted. One, two, three. The pie cooled between you. At six seconds, a ground beacon reported no key response. At nine, a second did the same. Eleven seconds, and still nothing from the orbital unit but a blank field.

She said your old project shorthand, barely more than breath. “Abort shadow?”

“Could be.” You watched the physical channel, not her. “Wait.”

At twelve seconds, two marks arrived together. The key store returned a permanent null. The pressure seal opened. A new object appeared on civilian tracking, separating slowly from the platform.

The armed lattice had ejected.

You checked the independent observers. Both matched. No targeting path remained; no ground command could restore one. Its armed mode was gone.

“Key destroyed,” you said. “Lattice separate and inert. Disarmament confirmed.”

“My office confirms,” the Prime Minister said. “The call is ending now.”

The line clicked dead.

For a while the only voices came through the hostage feed: a medic asking where it hurt, someone demanding a phone, an officer saying all six were present. Your former colleague missed her chair on the first attempt, caught its back, and sat.

At five twelve, vehicles turned into the narrow street below. No immunity had been discussed. She watched their blue-white lights pass across the ceiling, then put the cozy back over the tea.

“It won’t stay hot,” you said.

“No.” Her eyes remained on the window. “Would you give a statement?”

“A factual one.”

“Yes.”

“I’ll say you confined them to force an agreement.”

She nodded once. This time she did not correct your wording.

Heavy steps entered the building. She moved the cake knife away from the edge of the table and placed both hands flat beside her plate, visible from the doorway. The green cardigan, the leaf barrette, the carefully poured tea: none of it made her harmless.

Someone struck the door and ordered it opened.

Your former colleague looked at your half-finished pie. “You can take that with you.”

“I’m staying.”

She rose to answer the door. On the four small screens, the crew remained with counsel, the court receipt remained valid, the satellite remained disarmed, and all six former hostages stood beyond the outer line.

stories.title: Where No Unicorn Stands
stories.prompt: You are a unicorn and the only son of a newly crowned queen. Days after your mother's coronation, you are kidnapped by the Pegasi and taken to their kingdom in the clouds.
stories.body:
# Where No Unicorn Stands

I woke because my foreleg dropped through the sky.

Cloud closed around it, cold and almost wet, then let it pass. The only thing that stopped the rest of me was a rope net drawn hard beneath my ribs. Its knots bit through my coronation blanket. Above me, wings struck the dark in staggered beats. Below me hung a country without a bottom: moonlit folds, black wells, and, very far down, a scatter of lamps along a river I knew.

I kicked for ground. The net swung. One of the wingbeats faltered.

“Stop.” The voice came from ahead and above. “Forelegs in. Horn to your right.”

I kicked again.

The net tipped far enough for my shoulder to slide against its rim. Cloud swallowed my dangling hoof to the knee. No bank of mist caught it. Nothing did.

“There is no footing here,” the voice said. “The cords hold you. Use them.”

That was harder to understand than being stolen. Four days earlier I had stood beside my mother while the crown settled between her ears, and every unicorn in the hall had lowered a horn to us. Since then I had slept badly under embroidered blankets, answered questions nobody had asked me the week before, and learned that even breakfast could become an occasion. None of it had prepared me for a world through which my body could fall.

I hooked both forelegs over the net rope.

“Banking left,” the voice said.

“Who are you?”

“Left now.”

The Pegasi tilted together. My stomach remained behind while the net swept sideways. I shut my eyes, which only made the wingbeats larger.

When we leveled, I tried the words that had opened doors since the coronation. “I am the queen’s only son and witnessed heir. By her crown, you will return me unharmed.”

The Pegasus ahead glanced back. Moonlight edged a leather flight hood and the rigid line of his jaw. He flew in the lead harness; the other ropes ran from his chest to the four bearers around me.

“Save your breath,” he said. “Climb coming.”

He had heard every word. That frightened me more than if he had not.

They carried me until the river lamps disappeared. Dawn found us inside the storm my mother had rooted over the valley. It should have been pouring there, making dark coins in the dust and filling the stone channels between the orchards. Instead its rain remained around us: gray chambers, sudden white corridors, blue-black bulges that shuddered when the Pegasi passed.

Shapes emerged from it. Towers coiled upward on braided cloud. Bridges, stretched thin as old wool, joined terraces crowded with wings. A whole kingdom had been made out of what would not hold one of my hooves.

The captain gave his first explanation when the nearest tower showed daylight through its lower wall.

“Your queen stopped our storm.”

“She called rain to dying fields.”

“She nailed our city over them.”

“Then speak to her.”

His wings shortened their stroke for the descent. “We tried.”

The landing platform looked solid until they lowered the net. White flagstones pressed against my hind hooves. I put weight on them, grateful enough to gasp.

The stones opened like breath.

I plunged chest-deep. Pegasi shouted. Ropes snapped taut beneath my forelegs, wrenching my shoulders, while my hindquarters sank into luminous cold. The captain seized the back of my blanket in his teeth. Three others hauled upward. For a moment the sky was inside my mouth and ears, tasting of metal.

“A sling,” a new voice ordered. “Not another net. Bring the audience sling.”

“The western seam is taking everyone,” somebody answered.

“Then strip the canopy poles. Move.”

The speaker was an older mare with narrow wings and a chain of plain iron links around one foreleg. She came close enough to see me but did not touch me. “Can you breathe?”

“Return me.”

“Can you breathe?”

I pulled air past the rope crushing my chest. “Yes.”

“Did you strike your head?”

“Under my mother’s—”

“Look at me.” Her eyes tracked mine. “Did you?”

“No.”

The captain landed beside her, sides heaving. “Regent, the lower quarter has hours. We need his horn at the binding.”

She did not look away from me. “Under whose order did you seize him?”

“I had twenty-seven crews lose their roosts last night.”

“That is not an order.”

“The council debated while the nursery floor thinned.”

“Did he consent to come?”

The captain folded his wings too sharply. “No.”

The regent looked then. “So you have brought me a crime and attached our survival to it.”

“I brought the one horn that can loosen a fresh royal claim.”

“You brought a prince who cannot stand in the room where you intend to bargain with him.” She turned to the Pegasi wrestling dismantled poles through a doorway. “Food too. Something he can eat, not cloudfruit.”

The audience sling hung from four poles laid across two facing galleries. It was wide enough for me to lie in, padded under the breast, and humiliating in ways the cargo net had been too frightening to achieve. Beneath its woven floor, the court chamber descended through layer after layer of translucent cloud. Pegasi moved below us as dim shadows. At the edge of sight, parts of the city sloughed away in silent white sheets.

The regent asked questions as workers tightened the sling: when my mother had taken the crown, where the storm had been when she claimed it, whether her horn still touched the coronation stone. She stopped each answer before I could dress it in ceremony.

“Four days,” she repeated. “Then the root is still dividing.”

“My mother did not know you lived here.”

“I asked what she knew, not what you hope.”

The captain scraped one hoof against the cloud floor. It held him as turf would hold me. “A direct descendant can slacken the claim until it travels again. He makes one cut. We send the storm home after.”

“Home where?” I asked. “Up? Down?”

He pointed with one wing toward the vanishing lower city. “Anywhere but fixed.”

The regent’s gaze followed his. “One cut drops the stored rain.”

“It also saves us.”

“And drowns the valley under us.” I had become very still in the sling. “You carried me here to choose which kingdom falls.”

The captain’s answer came after one wingbeat too many. “I carried you here because ours was already falling.”

The regent ordered him out before he could turn that into a defense. She ordered guards at the sling, then changed her mind and ordered no guards within horn reach. She sent another message toward the ground and made the messenger repeat the route back to her. None of this was freedom. A braided tether still ran from the sling to an iron ring in the gallery. But the cup put before me held oat mash, not a speech, and the worker who set it down only said, “Careful, the bowl isn’t as solid as it looks.”

I ate because terror had made me hungry.

By afternoon, the sling ropes had rubbed two raw tracks behind my forelegs. The harness-keeper found them without asking where it hurt. She was a broad Pegasus with one primary feather missing from her right wing and wax rubbed into the fur around both knees. She slid a flat measuring strip under each rope.

“Too tight,” she said.

“It kept him in,” the captain said from the gallery.

“A knot can keep a sack in. He has shoulders.” She bit through a lashing and retied it with two quick pulls. “Lift your chin.”

I did not.

“Or keep the throat rub. Your throat.”

I lifted it. She fitted a padded guard along my horn, leaving the point bare. Her talk stayed with buckles and skin. Two feathers’ room at the chest. A hoof’s width behind the foreleg. Never trust a wet strap merely because it had stopped squeaking. When she asked whether I needed water, it sounded like one more measurement.

“I need to know if my mother received your messages.”

“Then you need someone else.”

“Did they come back?”

She tested the new knot with her full weight. “Some.”

“Show me.”

The captain said, “No.”

The harness-keeper said, “He can look while I move him.”

“He is not leaving the court.”

“Then his skin comes off here.” She looked at the frayed sling, not at either of us. “Your choice.”

They moved me in a maintenance cradle hung beneath her body. My hooves rested in separate loops; her belly and the cradle’s webbing made a low ceiling over my head. It should have felt more degrading than the sling. Instead the heat of a living body steadied me. I could hear how her breath changed before every turn.

She took me through kitchen ways where steam condensed on the walls and cooks braced pots between their knees. Pegasi folded their wings to let us pass. One complained that somebody had used the salt scoop for resin. Another pushed a heel of brown bread into the cradle and told me to chew before the next climb. Nobody asked me to save them.

The returned messages filled a sorting rack beside an outer hatch. I knew our palace ribbon: green, with a narrow gold edge. Six bundles wore it. Their wax seals were unbroken. Across each had been brushed the same gray mark.

“What does that mean?” I asked.

“No descent,” the harness-keeper said. “The rooted edge threw them back.”

“So she never saw them.”

“It means they did not reach your border riders. Keep your right hoof inside.”

“You said—”

“I said what the mark means.” She ducked under a beam. “Right hoof.”

I pulled it in just before the cradle scraped the wall.

Beyond the message hatch, a pale vertical crease ran through the storm. Rain glittered inside it, close enough that I smelled wet stone from the country below. My horn prickled. The sensation was familiar: the soft resistance of my mother’s magic when she set a ward over a door and let me open it from the other side.

There. A way out that did not require a Pegasus.

I waited until the harness-keeper turned to receive a replacement buckle. Then I drove my horn through the crease.

The storm tore.

Not widely. The opening was no longer than my neck. It was enough. The passage wall peeled outward, taking a section of terrace with it. A cook vanished in the white collapse. Wings hammered. A pot spun past, shedding broth in round drops.

“Horn out!” the harness-keeper shouted.

I froze.

“Out. Now, not down.”

I jerked backward. The captain plunged through the tear and came up beneath the cook, taking the cook’s weight across his back. Two workers caught the terrace edge with their wing-wakes. The harness-keeper slammed her shoulder into my cradle to keep it from turning.

“Close your eyes,” she said.

“I can help.”

“You are twisting the chest strap. Eyes closed. Breathe while I fix it.”

Her directions gave me three small things to do. I did them. When I opened my eyes, the cook was clinging to the passage, the captain’s left wing shook with strain, and the pale crease had become a dark wet scar. Far below, a sudden hammer of rain struck one bare patch of valley and ran brown over its banks.

My one hard cut had done that.

The captain landed and shoved the rescued cook toward the doorway. He looked at me, mouth open, but whatever accusation came first did not survive his need for air.

“I thought it was a passage,” I said.

“It is,” the harness-keeper said. “For water.”

The captain folded his trembling wing. “Back to court. Short route.”

He did not tell me I had proved him right. For that much, at least, I was grateful.

The storm began to shear after sunset. I knew it first through the cradle: every third wingbeat landed at a different angle. The harness-keeper stopped twice to shorten lines. By the time we reached the court, one gallery had been evacuated, and the audience sling swung empty over a widening shaft.

The regent stood beside its tether ring. “How much time?” she asked.

“To save the city?” said the captain. “Less than an hour.”

“To carry him to ground.”

His ears tipped back. “With which crews?”

“Yours.”

“If we turn from the upper seam, it parts.”

“Will your route reach the mountain?”

“Yes, but—”

“Then prepare it.”

The captain stared at her. Around us the court filled with clipped reports: east bridge empty, nursery moved, two bearers missing, rain load rising. The regent took the knife from the harness-keeper’s tool belt.

“Regent,” the captain said, “that tether is our claim.”

“It is evidence.” She cut the braided rope tying my cradle to the court. The loose end whipped through the iron ring and vanished into whiteness. “Carry him home.”

No bargain. No promise extracted. The lower quarter could dissolve, and she had given away the only body they believed might prevent it.

The harness-keeper began changing my cradle into a riding harness. I watched the cut end of the tether swing beneath me.

“Wait,” I said.

Nobody did; the floor lurched, and waiting had become dangerous.

“There are three moving seams,” I said louder. Fear made each word a separate object. “I can loosen them. Lightly. Not the root. Three releases, while we descend.”

The captain stopped fastening his breastplate. “You tried lightly once.”

“I tried to escape.”

The regent asked, “What changes now?”

“You released me.” The old ceremonial cadence pressed up when I needed plain speech, each clause wanting witnesses. “I offer aid bounded by my consent: three seams, on a homeward course, if my mother breaks contact with the coronation stone before the last. If you turn me back toward the city or fasten another tether, my offer ends.”

The captain glanced toward the upper towers, then toward the dark gap where the mountain lay beyond the storm. He could not make himself look at me.

“Homeward course,” he said. “Rig him to me.”

The harness-keeper put me on the captain’s back. Leather crossed my chest and belly; loops took my legs without binding them. He was smaller under me than he had looked beside the net. Every breath widened his ribs against mine.

“If he slips?” one bearer asked.

“He will not,” the harness-keeper said.

“That was not my question.”

She passed the bearer an emergency line. “Then keep this out of his horn.”

We flew.

The first seam raced down the storm’s outer face, a silver wrinkle in black vapor. The captain called distances, never looking back. “Twenty lengths. Ten. Brace.” The regent’s fliers beat above and below us, their wakes pulling the cloud skin tight. Rain bulged behind it.

“Now,” said the captain.

I touched the seam with my horn and drew a line no longer than my ear.

Cold seized my teeth. The root fought to remain one thing. Then it yielded by a fraction. Rain streamed out behind us in a narrow curtain, not down upon one field but slanting across miles of thirsty dark. The city lifted. I felt the change through the captain’s spine.

“One,” he said. “Turning.”

No praise. The route was already beneath his next instruction.

The second seam moved faster and lower. Wind flattened his mane into my eyes. The harness-keeper flew at our left, watching the straps rather than the rain.

“Chest is walking,” she called.

“Hold,” the captain shouted.

I held my horn away from the seam. He had meant my body.

The loose strap slid across his wing root. His left wing lost half a stroke. We dropped. The mountain lamps leapt upward, then disappeared behind cloud. Somebody screamed “Line,” and the bearer cast the emergency rope. It struck my horn guard and snagged.

“Don’t cut!” the captain barked.

I went rigid. Cut nothing. Move nothing. Be literal or kill a kingdom.

The harness-keeper slammed into our side and bit through the rope above the snag. “Your right knee,” she shouted at me. “Press down.”

“He said don’t—”

“Knee. Down.”

I pressed. My weight shifted off the captain’s damaged wing. His next stroke caught air; the following one caught more. We skimmed the seam so close that rain needled my face.

The captain did not have breath for a full command. “Horn. Two.”

I scored the second release.

Rain burst outward. The fliers below us vanished behind silver. The captain’s left wing shuddered but kept its rhythm, and the harness-keeper wedged the wandering chest strap beneath my knee where I could pin it.

“Keep that,” she said.

“I am.”

“You weren’t.”

We descended around the storm’s edge toward the mountain. With two seams open, the cloud city no longer sagged in one direction. Its lowest terraces remained ragged, some gone entirely, but the towers drew upward on the Pegasi wakes. Below, rain spread through two long bands. The river swelled within its banks.

At the exchange ridge, a line of unicorns stood with lowered horns. Their armor flashed whenever lightning moved inside the cloud. My mother waited ahead of them beside the coronation stone, her horn touching the wet white surface. The root ran from it into the storm as a green-gold cord only our kind could see.

She saw the captain carrying me. She saw the trailing strap, his failing wing, the Pegasi around us.

“Bows down,” she called.

Nobody moved.

My mother stepped between the armed line and the cliff. “All of them. Down.”

Horn tips rose from their aim. Bowstrings slackened. Only then did she turn away from me. She put one forehoof against the coronation stone and wrenched her horn free.

The green-gold cord snapped back into the storm.

The captain stumbled in the air as the released root changed the wind. The final seam opened beneath us, broad and pulsing.

“Three?” he managed.

It was not a command anymore. It was all the question he could carry.

I lowered my horn. This time the magic gave under its own weight. I guided the opening along the seam while the captain flew the curve, and the stored storm descended in a wide gray veil. Rain reached the valley, the ridges, and the cloud kingdom’s tattered underside. The city drifted free, turning slowly toward the dark country beyond the mountains.

The captain reached turf before his left wing failed.

Mountain grass struck my hooves through the harness loops. Real weight rose into my bones. I had imagined the relief so often that the truth of it surprised me: mud between my toes, stones pressing one heel, the slope refusing to let me through. The captain folded under us. I tore at the buckles with my teeth until the harness-keeper landed and pushed me aside.

“Third pin,” she said. “Not the shiny one. Third.”

My mother arrived first and found it before I did. She pulled the pin, rolled the captain onto his sound side, then worked the chest leather away from my raw skin. The armed line kept its distance because she had told it to. The regent landed farther upslope with three fliers and no court behind her.

Nobody discussed peace in the rain.

We took shelter in a shepherd’s hut just below the ridge. It smelled of damp wool and last winter’s ashes. My mother cleaned the rope burns with boiled water while the harness-keeper wrapped the captain’s wing around a split of roof lath. The regent counted who had returned. A valley guard set down bread, hard cheese, and a pot of beans, then left when the queen looked at the weapons still on his back.

The captain woke once while his wing was being bound.

“City?” he asked.

“Moving east,” the regent said. Her voice had shortened to exhaustion. “Lower homes lost. No count yet.”

He swallowed. “Route held?”

“Eat later,” the harness-keeper told him. “Talk less now.” She pulled the bandage firm. He obeyed.

My mother removed the last strap from behind my foreleg. Fur and a little skin came with it. Her mouth tightened, but she did not ask me to comfort her. She did not ask whether the Pegasi had hurt me, as if one answer could hold the net, the sling, the bread, the cut tether, and the captain’s back.

“The stone?” I asked.

“Cold,” she said. “I released it before I knew you would reach us.”

Across the hut, the captain watched the rain tick from the roof. “I took you,” he said. The rest failed somewhere between his ribs and his teeth.

“Yes,” I said.

The harness-keeper shoved a folded blanket under his bandaged wing. “Don’t roll onto that.”

The regent broke the bread into uneven pieces. My mother passed the largest to me.

“When you can,” she said.

She meant the whole account. The six sealed bundles. The torn terrace. The cut tether and everything after. My mouth tasted of rain and old rope. I could not begin while the captain’s bandage was still being tied.

“Not yet,” I said.

My mother nodded and pushed the beans closer. The harness-keeper ate standing up. The regent counted the bread again and gave the captain her piece when she thought nobody watched.

I put all four hooves on the packed earth floor. Then I ate.

stories.title: The Other Twin
stories.prompt: You and your twin sister were born fused into a single body. Everything was going surprisingly well until you hit puberty and your body began to display both female and male traits.
stories.body:
# The Other Twin

When we were little, brushing our teeth took ninety seconds. My sister worked the caps, I ran the tap, and both hands knew the route from cup to mouth without either of us looking down. She spat first. I leaned us in. She caught the towel while I shut off the water. We were so good at it that our mother sometimes stood in the bathroom door and watched with the soft, useless pride other parents saved for piano recitals.

By fourteen, the same sink could hold us hostage.

That morning, my sister had the left hand pressed flat below our collarbone. The ache had started as a bruise with no bruise, then spread until the seam of our pajama shirt hurt. Our chest looked fuller beneath the cotton. Under my own chin, three dark hairs had become eleven. I had counted them while she slept and then felt ashamed, though not ashamed enough to stop being pleased.

“Razor first,” I said.

“Soft bra first.”

Both were waiting beside the soap. She moved the left hand toward the folded bra. I moved the right toward the razor. Our shoulders turned in opposite directions, and the pull through our spine made both arms stop.

“It takes thirty seconds.”

“It hurts now.”

I looked at her in the mirror. Her hair was pinned away from her face with two yellow clips. Mine stuck up where I had slept on it. Between our necks, the pajama collar had twisted sideways.

“Fine,” I said, but too late to make the word kind.

We put on the bra. It did not belong to her half of us, because there was no half to put it on. The band went around our ribs. I felt the pressure when she fastened it. She felt me stiffen.

Afterward, she held the razor under the hot tap while I shaved eleven hairs from my chin. She did not complain. That was how I decided we had been fair.

I was still using that arithmetic in October.

The next time the sink held us was the morning we caught the early bus. At the mirror, she chose a green shirt that curved instead of hanging from us. I kept the shadow on my jaw. This was supposed to count as one choice each. She tugged the hem smooth; I opened our jacket halfway. We looked like an argument assembled from the lost-and-found.

“The jacket’s crooked,” she said.

“The shirt’s doing that.”

“No, your hand is.”

I fixed it. Our mother, kneeling by the front door with one of our shoes between her knees, pulled the laces tight.

“Bus in six minutes.”

“Five,” I said.

“Then you’d better not spend one correcting me.” She double-knotted the lace and stood. “Lunch is in the front pocket. Pads are in the inside one.”

My sister said, “I put them there.”

“Good. Move.”

Outside, wet leaves pasted themselves to the pavement. Walking had once been our best trick. We did not each own a leg; a step began as a shift we both had to feel coming. When we agreed on the destination, the agreement traveled down our back and gathered itself into knees, ankles, toes. Since our hips had begun changing, the old signals arrived at the wrong angle. We had to think about curbs.

At the bus shelter, a man in a reflective vest held the gate for us. His eyes went to our chest, then to my sister’s face.

“Morning, girls.”

“Morning,” I said.

My sister’s head turned toward me. “He wasn’t talking to you.”

“He said girls.”

“Exactly.”

The bus hissed at the curb. I shifted forward before she did. She was still looking back at the man when our left foot met the step, and the right struck the metal edge. Pain went up both legs. We caught the rail with both hands and hung there for one ugly second, our weight behind us and the line of students behind that.

“You okay?” the driver asked.

“We’re fine,” I said.

“I’m not,” my sister said at the same time.

The driver got out of her seat. She planted one hand under our elbow, waited while my sister looked down at the step, and said, “Ready?”

My sister nodded. I waited for the breath we used before stairs. We climbed.

At the back of the bus, she examined the darkening patch on our shin.

“I wasn’t trying to trip us,” she said.

“I know.”

“You moved.”

“The bus was here.”

She pulled the jacket closed over the green shirt. “The question can get here before your answer once in a while.”

I watched rain stitch the window. By lunch, I had converted the fall into a problem with preventable inputs: wet pavement, changed balance, distraction. I did not include myself. I did not yet understand that answering for both of us was also a kind of movement.

The third time the sink stopped us, there was blood in our underwear.

Our mother had explained what might happen. There was a box beneath the sink, pain medicine in the cabinet, a heating pad folded in the linen closet. Preparedness turned out to be small beside the fact itself. The cramps had woken both of us before dawn, squeezing low in our shared belly and releasing just long enough for hope to become stupid.

My sister braced both hands on the porcelain. “Get Mom.”

“We know what to do.”

“Get her anyway.”

I called. Our mother came in wearing one slipper and carrying her glasses. She took in the underwear, my sister’s face, my face.

“Bathroom first,” she said. “Then heat. School can wait.”

She showed my sister where to place the pad and gave me the job of holding the waistband out of the way. Later, with the heating pad across our abdomen, my sister asked for toast. I wanted the curtains shut. She watched a cooking video with the sound low while I tried to sleep through cramps that felt insultingly ordinary.

Over the next three months, ordinary things multiplied. Shirts that fit at breakfast chafed by last period. Sweat gathered beneath new folds of skin. My voice dropped more than my sister’s, though hers broke sometimes in the middle of a word and made her go silent. Hair thickened on our legs and under our arms; more appeared along my jaw and a faint strip above her lip. She plucked that strip. I asked her not to use my good tweezers. She said we had one face each but apparently communal tweezers.

We still made jokes. We fought over music while folding laundry. She made me watch six episodes of a baking competition and then fell asleep before the final. I finished it and lied about who won. She knew before breakfast.

But the old system of my day and your day had depended on choices ending when the day did. The green shirt came off. My stubble could be shaved. Our chest did not flatten overnight, and bleeding did not become hers because the calendar had her handwriting on it.

Our mother called a specialist after each of us asked her separately. She showed us the appointment time on her phone.

“Thursday, three forty,” she said. “I can collect you from school.”

“What kind of specialist?” my sister asked.

“The kind who read the scans your regular doctor sent and admitted they need more scans.”

“That’s not a kind.”

“It’s the kind we have Thursday.”

At the clinic, the receptionist handed us a clipboard with one form. Our mother handed it back.

“Two patients,” she said.

The receptionist looked at the single insurance number, then at us. “There’s one chart.”

“Put two questionnaires in it.”

The woman considered the waiting room behind us, where no one had volunteered to become less impatient. Then she found another form.

We completed them one at a time because handwriting required both hands to agree. My sister answered first. I steadied the page and let her choose the words. Under WHAT CHANGES ARE TROUBLING YOU? she wrote, People look at him and decide I’m not here. Then she added, Hair. Voice. Speed.

I wrote, Chest development. Menstruation. Unpredictability of final traits.

She read over my shoulder. “Final traits.”

“It asks what troubles me.”

“You make us sound like a building proposal.”

“You wrote speed.”

“Speed is what I mean.”

The clinician brought the two forms into the examination room and placed them side by side on her desk. She spoke slowly, but not in the sugary way adults sometimes used when they thought our body had made our minds younger.

“I’ll ask some questions twice,” she said. “Not because I expect the answers to match.”

“We’ve already compared—” I began.

She lifted one hand, not high. “You can go first when I ask you.” She turned to my sister. “What change would you most want to slow right now?”

“The hair. On our body, and this.” My sister touched above her lip. “And my voice. It goes wrong and people laugh before I finish.”

The clinician made a note. “What change would you be sorry to slow?”

My sister’s hand moved to our sternum, then dropped. “Our chest. Maybe. I don’t know yet.”

“All right.”

Then the clinician turned to me.

I had prepared. “If development continues at the current rate, I want to know the likely range of outcomes, the probability of further breast growth, whether menstruation will regularize, and which interventions preserve later options.”

My sister shifted in the chair. Our knee knocked the underside of the desk.

The clinician waited. “Which change would you most want to slow right now?”

“Breast growth.”

“And which would you be sorry to slow?”

I rubbed the place beneath my jaw that was rough by afternoon. “My voice. The hair.”

That answer looked very small beside all the ones I had brought, and it was the first useful thing I said in the room.

The clinician showed us a diagram made from our own scans. Most of it was lines and pale shapes that meant little to me. She kept her pen on the parts that mattered. One circulation. Several kinds of tissue responding at different rates. In our particular body, she said, a monitored course of temporary suppression might slow the signals driving further changes. It would not assign one set of effects to my sister and another to me. It would not reverse what had happened. If we stopped, development might resume, but she could not promise its timing or direction.

“How much time would it give us?” I asked.

“I can give you monitoring intervals. I can’t give you a guaranteed future.”

“But on average—”

“Your scans aren’t an average.” She checked the clock. “There are also reasons to continue without medication. There are costs either way. I don’t need a decision today.”

My sister had gone still. The clinician laid her pen sideways across the diagram and waited.

Finally my sister said, “If we pause it, I don’t stop being a girl?”

The clinician’s gaze stayed on her. “The medication would act on your shared body. I’m not treating either of your identities.”

My sister nodded once. I had a better, more complete version of the question in my head. For once I left it there.

The worst fight happened six days later, over a charcoal shirt.

It was large enough not to pull across our chest. That was why I had put it on the bed for the school winter concert. My sister had chosen a red top with a square collar and sleeves that made lifting our arms difficult. Neither was formal enough for her and both were too noticeable for me.

“Charcoal,” I said. “We’ll be onstage for nine minutes. It reduces the number of things people can decide from a distance.”

“About you.”

“About both of us. Fewer wrong guesses overall.”

She picked up the red top with our left hand. “I want this one.”

“You’ll hate it when they stare.”

“They stare now.”

I began unbuttoning the shirt we wore. She did not help. The right hand fumbled the third button while the left stayed closed around red fabric.

“Can we solve the immediate problem?” I asked. “Nine minutes, lower visibility, no restricted shoulders. Then in January we reassess after the next appointment.”

“You’ve spent me again.”

“What does that mean?”

“My shirt. My chest. My nine minutes. They all disappear inside your total.”

“There is no version where either of us gets everything.”

She looked down at the red sleeve gathered in our fist. “I know.”

“Then help me.”

“No.”

I pulled the open side of our shirt. She held the other. The cloth tightened behind our necks. We had undressed through arguments before, but not with both of us insisting our body go somewhere different. Our elbow caught under a sleeve. Balance tipped toward the dresser, and one knee locked while the other tried to bend. The corner rushed at us in the mirror.

“Stop,” my sister said.

I was still talking—something about falling if she would not coordinate—when our palm slapped the dresser top hard enough to rattle the hairbrushes.

“Stop.”

This time I did. We stood half inside the shirt, breathing too fast. Our shoulder burned where the seam had twisted. The concert was in forty minutes. The red top lay on the floor.

Our mother appeared at the door. She saw the trapped elbow and came close, then waited.

“Help?” she asked.

My sister said yes. I could not get enough breath for the word, so I nodded.

Our mother freed the cloth from behind our necks. She did not ask who had started it. She laid the charcoal shirt on the chair, put the red top beside it, and set one of her soft black cardigans between them.

“I’ll call the school,” she said.

“We can still make it,” I said.

“You can. You don’t have to. Tell me in ten minutes.”

After she left, my sister sat us on the bed. The sudden drop made the mattress springs complain.

I tried again. “If we list the costs—”

“I need it to stop getting faster.”

“That doesn’t decide the shirt.”

“I’m not deciding the shirt.” She rubbed our caught shoulder. “I need this to stop getting faster.”

The clinic packet was on the desk. Until then, I had treated a pause as her proposal and therefore as something I had to measure against my losses. I pictured my voice fixed where it was, a beard that might never become more than a little roughness along my jaw. I pictured our chest continuing to change while I collected better numbers. Neither picture belonged to her. Neither belonged only to me.

“I don’t want to lose what’s happening to my voice,” I said.

“I know.”

“And you don’t want to lose—”

“Don’t finish it.”

Our hands rested open on our knees. I let them.

We missed the concert. Our mother brought dinner upstairs on a tray because neither of us wanted the kitchen table. She put down two forks with one plate of pasta.

“Ten-thirty bedtime,” she said. “Appointment packet’s on the desk. Cardigan can go back in my closet tomorrow.”

At the door, she stopped.

“Mom?” I said.

“What?”

I had wanted her to tell us what was fair. My sister was watching the steam rise from the pasta.

“Can we use your phone after dinner?” I asked. “For two recordings.”

“Yes.” She left the door open a hand’s width.

We made the recordings separately. Privacy was impossible, but authorship was not. My sister spoke first while I kept my mouth shut and looked at the dark window.

“I like our chest changing,” she said into the phone. “I don’t like bleeding, but that isn’t the same thing. I hate the hair on my face. I hate people hearing my voice crack and looking at him. I don’t want every week to take something before I know if I wanted it. I want a pause.”

She stopped the recording herself.

On mine, I began with likely outcomes, crossed them out aloud, and began again.

“I like my voice. I like shaving, which is stupid because I’ve cut my chin twice. I don’t want more chest growth. I don’t want another period. I keep saying later will be easier to decide, but I’m the one asking for forecasts while everything keeps happening. I want a pause too. Not forever. Now.”

At the second consultation, the clinician listened to both recordings. She asked my sister whether “pause” still meant the monitored temporary course they had discussed. Then she asked me. Two yeses entered the same chart. Our mother scheduled the first follow-up before we left.

The treatment was not a clean door shutting. Weeks later, our chest still pressed against the soft bra. My chin still needed shaving. Blood might come again before the clinician could tell whether the course was slowing anything. At school, strangers continued to pick one of us from a distance and misplace the other.

But the mornings stopped feeling like a race against a body that had started without us.

At the sink in February, my sister set down the tweezers beside my razor.

“Hold still,” she said.

“You’ve got one.”

“It’s one too many.”

I leaned our weight toward the mirror while she plucked the dark hair above her lip. Her eyes watered.

“Done,” I said.

“I know.” She rinsed the tweezers. “Your turn.”

She held our chin steady while I shaved. Halfway through, our mother called that the bus was in four minutes.

“Five,” I called back.

My sister reached for the yellow hair clips. “Don’t start.”

I wiped the remaining soap from my jaw and left one side rough. She clipped back only half her hair. We grabbed our bag, missed the towel, and went.

stories.title: One Night's Mercy
stories.prompt: "Please," the queen begs on her knees, "save that dragon from my daughter."
stories.body:
# One Night's Mercy

“Please, save that dragon from my daughter.”

Queen Urrava was on both knees in the scale and soot of Imer Quast’s forge. Two royal guards stood behind her, wet to the shoulders. Hovan Setch stood with them, rain running off his cropped hair. All three had heard her, which meant she had not come to be forgiven in private.

Imer left the bellows open. The coal dimmed around the hinge strap he had been heating.

“Which dragon?”

Urrava’s hands rested palm-down on the floor. She had removed her rings. Careful, even now. Nothing metal to cut her when she knelt.

“Thelrax. Daziel has him in the north quarry. The throat is pierced, both wings are weighted, and she means to use a spear at first light.”

Hovan said, “I saw the wound before the rain closed the ridge. He can breathe. Fire, perhaps twice. Short.”

“How short?” Imer asked.

“Eight paces. Two bursts at most, from that wound. I may be wrong about how much strength he has left.”

“And the quarry road?”

“The bridge is under,” said the queen. “My riders cannot reach her before dawn. You can use the inspection chute.”

The chute Imer had cut through the hill when Daziel was still young enough to steal his chalk and draw wolves on new stone. The chute ended behind the quarry drums. It was narrow, steep, and meant for men who understood why a frayed rope could be worse than a cracked beam.

He looked past Urrava to the guards. “You came to order me back into service.”

“No. I came to bargain. If you go, your dismissal is rescinded, your forge levy ends, and the crown repays—”

“Keep it.”

“Then name what you require.”

“The truth she doesn’t have.”

Urrava’s gaze shifted once, toward Hovan. He did not help her.

Imer wiped his hands on his apron. “Daziel thinks her husband broke the nest seal against your instructions. That is why she can grieve him and still call his death a consequence of his own pride. You would not be kneeling here if that were true.”

Rain drummed on the forge hood. One guard swallowed.

Urrava rose no higher. “I authorized an armed survey.”

“Of a sealed nest.”

“Of the copper behind it.”

“The writ.”

“Imer—”

“The paper, or get out of my forge.”

Her balanced patience went out of her face. “Give it to him.”

The older guard unbuttoned his soaked coat and produced an oilskin packet. Inside lay a folded writ with the royal seal and Daziel’s husband’s name beneath the command to open, inspect, and secure. Urrava’s signature ran across the bottom. A second object dropped into Imer’s palm: a square iron key for the inspection gate, its teeth filed to the quarry’s old pattern.

“You kept the original,” he said.

“I kept the only proof that the command was mine.”

“And let the dead man carry the blame.”

“I let the court believe what it was prepared to believe.”

That was as near as Urrava came to saying she had chosen it.

Imer folded the writ small and put it inside his shirt. “You stay here.”

She stood. The guards almost moved to help and thought better of it. “Daziel will hear me.”

“She has heard you all her life. Tonight she needs to see the paper before she sees another royal face.”

“Bring her back.”

“I’m going to stop the rig. What Daziel does after that is hers.” Imer took his waxed coat from its peg. “Hovan. Lamp oil?”

“Half a flask.”

“Take the full one. And the thin hemp, not that court rope. Those knots have never been wet.”

Hovan exchanged the guards’ clean coil for the blackened line beside Imer’s door. Urrava called Imer’s name once, but by then he was testing the rope between both hands.

* * *

The storm had put a brown river through the lower lane. Imer and Hovan crossed it on the remains of a fence, then climbed the sheep track with their shoulders turned into the rain. Beyond the ridge, the abandoned quarry showed itself only when lightning filled its cut faces: three pale steps descending into blackness.

The inspection gate had swollen in its frame. Imer drove Urrava’s key in with his palm.

“Knot,” he said.

Hovan tied the lamp to his belt and the rope around a stone horn inside the gate.

Imer pulled it loose. “Again.”

“It held on the road.”

“The road wasn’t trying to peel you.”

Hovan retied it with the tail inside. This time Imer nodded.

They went down the chute backward, boots searching for iron rungs slick with seep water. The close stone took the storm’s noise and turned it into a steady grinding. Halfway down, Hovan’s lamp guttered.

“Oil,” Imer said.

“Wick first.”

“Why?”

“Oil’s full. Wick drowned.” Hovan pinched it higher with two nails. The light steadied. “You asked me to say when I know.”

“I did.”

“You usually dislike it.”

Imer put his foot on the next rung. “Usually I’m right.”

At the bottom they smelled Thelrax before they saw him: rain on hot stone, blood, and the bitter mineral stink of burned rope.

The chute opened behind the winch shed. Through missing boards, Imer saw the snare stretched over the quarry’s lowest shelf. Three anchor lines drew toward it from separate frames, all running over drums he had built. In their middle crouched a dragon the length of a freight wagon, dark hide slick against the limestone. The upper net bit across his shoulders. Its line also carried the short cable from a bolt through the loose skin beneath his jaw. Two sling nets lay over the folded wings, each loaded with quarried blocks and drawn tight to a side anchor.

His throat worked around every breath.

Above him, mounted on the loading gantry, a boar spear sat in a timber stock. Its iron head pointed down between the dragon’s shoulder blades. The counterweight hung over an old lifting shaft.

Princess Daziel stood at the firing lever with a hooded lantern at her feet. She wore no crown. A quarry coat covered her hunting leathers, and a coiled stay rope lay beside her boots.

“I heard the gate,” she said. “I expected my mother.”

Imer stepped through the shed door. “She sent something more useful.”

Daziel’s attention moved to Hovan, then to Imer’s hands. “No tools?”

“Plenty here if you haven’t ruined them.”

“I improved the rig.”

Imer followed the new cord from the spear’s trigger pin down the frame. It passed through two eyes and ended in a loop around the lower drum’s brake pawl.

Anger steadied Imer’s hands. “You coupled the spear to the lower brake.”

“If he pulls the downslope wing free, the drum turns and the spear drops.”

“The lower brake is the first release in the safe sequence.”

“Then don’t release it.”

Lightning showed Thelrax’s eye, open and fixed on them. He shifted one foreclaw. The three lines answered in different notes.

Hovan stayed beside the shed. He raised an empty hand, palm angled away. Approach. The dragon’s nostrils widened, but he did not strike.

Daziel said, “Make him put his head down.”

“I can show pain, space, danger, wait, and approach.”

“You told me a lowered head meant submission.”

“I told you he lowered it when the bolt hurt.” Hovan watched Thelrax’s jaw, not Daziel. “I don’t know a submission signal.”

“Make one.”

“No.”

The word did not challenge her. It ended the request.

Daziel looked back at Imer. “My husband entered the nest with six people. He broke the inner seal. The dragon killed him before the second person crossed. I saw the marks on the wall. One bite. Then, twelve days later, Thelrax flew over the east shelter and burned the roof while eight workers were inside. They had not gone near the nest.”

“I know what he did.”

“Do you? You were already dismissed.”

Imer took out the writ. “For opposing the raid.”

She did not reach for it. “He was ordered to survey a copper seam.”

“Read the bottom.”

Rain struck the paper as Daziel unfolded it. She put the lantern closer. Her eyes moved once through the command, a second time through the names, and stopped at Urrava’s signature.

Thelrax’s claws scraped downslope. One wing weight lifted a finger’s width and dropped.

Daziel refolded the writ along the wrong crease. “She signed this before he left.”

“Yes.”

“She told me he added the weapons himself.”

Imer said nothing.

“He did add them. The inventory proves it. But she sent him to break the seal.” Daziel pushed the paper back against Imer’s chest. “That changes her part. It does not change his neck in that nest. It does not change the shelter roof.”

“No.”

“Then stand clear.”

“Stand down until I inspect it.”

“No.”

“At dawn?”

“The crosswind falls. I get one clean thrust before his throat closes or he tears it wider. I will not leave him to pull loose over the lower camp.”

“Your crew?”

“Evacuated. Nine at the shepherd sheds, two at the bridge watch. I counted them out.”

“And you stay with a trigger tied into a brake that was never made to feel a wing.”

“I’ve held it since dusk.”

The certainty in her voice was not court certainty. It belonged to six wet hours with a lever under her hand.

Imer unbuckled his coat. “I need to go inside the frame.”

“No.”

“The upper line is rubbing. If it parts, you won’t get dawn.”

“I can fire before it parts.”

“Maybe. Or the lower drum turns first and fires for you. I can tell which if I touch the bearings.”

Daziel considered the gantry, the dragon, and the man who had once made her reset a rabbit snare six times because she kept hiding the knot where she could not inspect it. She shifted her grip to the firing lever.

“Go,” she said. “Hovan stays where I can see him.”

* * *

The frame had been built to lift blocks. Its braces were sized for dead weight, steady from first lift to last. Imer took a quarry bar from the rack and crawled beneath the lower drum.
