Water ticked off the axle housing. He put two fingers against the bearing cap and felt the cable creep one strand at a time.

“It’s moving,” he called.

“How much?” Daziel asked.

“Enough.”

“That is not a measure.”

“It will be when I find where it goes.”

Hovan edged toward the shelf. He showed wait: both hands low, the motion slow enough to stop before it became approach.

Thelrax’s head turned. The bolt cable scraped stone. For one breath he went still.

Then he pushed with both hind legs toward the open, descending quarry road.

The downslope wing cradle rose. The lower drum clicked against its pawl.

Daziel locked the firing lever against her hip. “He knows what that means.”

Hovan took longer to answer. “He sees open ground. He is loading toward it. I don’t know what he knows about the spear.”

“Signal wait again.”

“He refused it.”

“Again.”

Hovan did, because refusal once was not refusal forever. Thelrax opened his jaws. Blood threaded from the bolt wound. His chest swelled and stopped short. He dragged downslope another handspan.

“No more,” Hovan said.

Imer had reached the far side of the drum. Daziel’s added trigger cord looked loose from above. Underneath, where it crossed the old brake spring, it had bitten deep into the wet wood. The upper net line bore across that spring at an angle no drawing would have shown.

“Do not cut the upper net,” he said.

“That was your second release.”

“Not now. When it goes slack, the spring lifts the lower pawl. The spear fires.”

Daziel’s face changed very little. Her hand changed more, opening and closing once around the lever.

“Can you uncouple it?”

“If the load holds.”

The left upright gave a dry crack.

Everyone looked at it except Thelrax. He looked at the quarry road.

“Split above the brace,” Imer said. “Daziel, take the stay rope. Hovan, clear the road below him. Loose stone, tools, everything. He needs a straight downslope run with those weights.”

“If I clear it, he may take it,” Hovan said.

“Yes.”

Hovan looked at Daziel.

She wrapped the stay rope around her left forearm while her right hand remained on the lever. “Clear it.”

Hovan moved. He kicked wedges off the track, rolled a dropped maul into the drainage cut, and hauled a handcart sideways by its shaft. Thelrax followed him with one eye. When Hovan crossed in front of the dragon, the jaws opened again.

“Space,” Hovan said, first to them. Then he gave the broad retreating motion Thelrax had accepted before.

The dragon’s answer was fire.

It came broken around the throat bolt, a flat orange burst that reached the edge of the handcart and no farther: eight paces, perhaps less. Hovan dropped behind the stone wheel. Flame washed over the upper net. Imer smelled scorched hemp and hair.

The burst stopped. Thelrax coughed dark smoke and lowered his head, not in submission, not in anything Hovan could name.

“Hovan?” Imer called.

“Sleeve burned. Hand works.”

“Then move the cart.”

“I am moving it.” Hovan’s words came slowly now, with air between them. He rose behind the wheel and dragged the cart until the track lay clear.

The scorched upper net shrank. Its drum turned backward. The lower pawl began to climb.

Imer shoved his pry bar through the flywheel. It caught between two spokes and drove him shoulder-first into the frame. The wheel stopped with the bar pinned across his chest.

The split upright opened another inch.

“Imer,” Daziel said.

“Hold the stay.”

“It won’t hold both.”

He knew. The whole changed load had come into his arms: dragon, wet net, wing stone, spear spring, and every wet turn of Daziel’s new cord. If Daziel fired, Thelrax would collapse and the frame would settle. If she let the upright tear free, the flywheel would take Imer through it.

The spear carriage shuddered overhead.

“Firing now braces the leg,” Daziel said. A work call. No defense left in it.

“It does.”

“You cannot get out.”

“Not while the wheel turns.”

At the track, Hovan pulled the last coil of rope clear with his unburned hand. “Path is open. I think he will take it. I don’t know.”

Thelrax dug in. Downslope. The lower drum pressed harder against Imer’s bar.

Daziel looked at the spear, then at the red dump pin securing its bed over the empty shaft. The pin was six feet from her. To reach it she would have to release the stay rope. The upright would split before she could return.

“Imer.”

He had no useful answer. “Pin needs both hands. Twist left before you pull.”

She took her right hand from the firing lever and caught the dump pin. The trigger arm jumped but did not fall; the lower pawl, jammed against Imer’s flywheel, held it by half a tooth.

Then Daziel let the stay rope run from her left hand.

The upright tore. Imer’s pry bar bowed. Daziel twisted the pin left and hauled. It came out to the stop chain.

The spear bed tipped into the shaft. Timber, iron spear, and counterweight fell together. The sound went down for a long time before stone answered.

Freed of the counterweight, the trigger cord lashed across the frame. The flywheel took a quarter turn. Imer lost his feet.

Daziel caught the back of his belt with both hands. His ribs struck the axle, but the pry bar stayed between the spokes.

“Left anchor!” he gasped. “Not upper. Left.”

She seized the release maul and knocked the left wing pin through. The first sling line dropped slack, leaving its stones to drag instead of wrenching the wing upward. Imer dragged the bar backward one notch and found his knees.

“Right now.”

The second pin stuck. Daziel hit it once, reset her footing, and hit it square. The downslope sling line spilled loose.

Thelrax surged. The burned net tightened across his shoulders.

“Upper!”

Hovan was closer. He snatched the maul from the mud, but before he swung, he looked to Imer.

“Yes,” Imer said.

Hovan drove the upper pin out.

The net slipped over Thelrax’s back. For one moment the dragon remained crouched, unheld. Hovan showed approach, small and careful, toward the wound.

Thelrax bared his teeth.

Hovan stopped. “No approach.”

The dragon took the downslope road. The weighted wing slings skidded beside him for three strides, shedding blocks, before the loosened nets slipped clear. On the fourth stride he opened his wings. The torn throat made a hard, wet sound. He ran through it.

At the quarry lip, where the road dropped into the valley, Thelrax jumped.

He sank below the rim. Daziel moved to the edge, empty hands lifted as if they still held rope. A wing struck air once, twice. The dragon rose past the far face and went into the rain without turning toward them.

* * *

By dawn the storm had thinned to a cold mist. Thelrax crossed the western ridge low and uneven, then disappeared beyond it. Hovan would not call the flight safe. He would only say the dragon had cleared the rock.

Daziel sat on an overturned block while Imer wrapped Hovan’s forearm. The burn had blistered where the sleeve ended. Imer’s own ribs hurt when he pulled the knot tight.

“Not so tight,” Hovan said.

“You’ll swell.”

“Then leave two fingers.”

Imer left two.

Daziel had dried Urrava’s writ under the lamp. She read it again, folded it on its first creases, and put it inside her coat.

“The nine at the sheds,” Imer said. “Names.”

She gave them. Then the two bridge watchers. Hovan repeated the count while Imer marked eleven strokes in chalk on the winch shed door.

“I’m ending the hunt,” Daziel said. “If he comes at another occupied roof, I’ll answer that. I’m not following him from here.”

Imer nodded.

“I haven’t forgiven him.”

“I know.”

She pressed the writ flat beneath her palm. “I’m taking the long road back. She can read this with me.”

There was nothing useful Imer could add. He handed Daziel the dry end of Hovan’s bandage, and she tied it off.

Before any crew returned, they went back to the broken frame. The spear was gone, but the empty stock still held a cocked spring, and the trigger cord had wound itself twice around the lower axle. One turn of the drum could fire the carriage a second time into whoever stood at the rail.

Daziel held the lamp. Hovan found the oil hole. Imer set a blunt pin across the trigger housing and raised the maul.

“Foot back,” Daziel said.

He moved it. Hovan poured the oil. On the third blow, the pin bent flat.

stories.title: Coiled Together
stories.prompt: Everyone knows the serpentfolk lure travelers into their caves and devour them. When you wake wrapped tightly in the coils of one of their most feared queens, however, she seems less interested in eating you than in keeping you—and insists that you were the one who begged her not to let go.
stories.body:
# Coiled Together

I woke because I could not finish a breath.

Something warm and hard crossed my chest. Another band pinned my thighs. A third lay behind my shoulders, holding me against a body that shifted under me with slow muscular corrections. The cave was dark except for a clay lamp on a shelf. Its flame showed overlapping black-green scales, each as broad as two fingers, curving around me and continuing beyond the light.

Everyone on the north road knew what serpentfolk did with travelers underground. The stories disagreed about whether they swallowed boots.

I tried to reach my knife. My arm did not move.

The coil across my ribs tightened when I struggled. Not much. Enough.

“Loosen.” My first attempt scraped out too softly. I swallowed and tried again. “Loosen me.”

The pressure eased at once. The band across my chest lifted until I could drag in a full breath. Cool cave air burned my throat.

“More?” a woman asked beside my ear.

Her common speech was plain, the voice low from effort rather than softness.

“Release me.”

The coils began to move. I felt myself tip toward open air and clutched at the first solid thing under my hand.

“There is a drop to your left,” she said. “I am putting you on the hide.”

One of her two arms came beneath my shoulders. The other steadied my knees while her body unwound in stages: chest, hips, ankles last. She set me on a folded hide three paces from the ledge and took both hands away.

I rolled onto my elbows. The cave swayed. My knife and belt lay beside a wet pack, close enough to reach. I dragged the knife free before I looked at her.

She had drawn herself into a wide curve along the edge of the shelf. Seven metres, perhaps, from the human-shaped rise of her ribs to the blunt end of her tail. A storm-grey wrap crossed one shoulder and covered the join of her arms to her scaled trunk. Below it, a dark stain spread along her right flank. One of the serpentfolk’s feared queens, if the notched copper bands on both forearms meant what the caravan guards said they meant.

Behind her, a smaller serpentfolk knelt over an open medicine case. The attendant held a strip of cloth in both hands and watched the queen’s wound, not my knife.

The queen said, “You asked me not to let go.”

My grip tightened. “I asked you to wrap me like that?”

“You said, ‘Don’t drop me.’ Several times. I was carrying you out of the flooded lower basin.”

“I don’t remember a basin.”

“I know.”

“Then how convenient for you.”

The attendant pressed the cloth to the queen’s flank. The queen’s fingers closed once on the stone, then opened.

“That request governed the climb,” she said. “You asked for release now. I released you.”

Rain boomed somewhere inside the mountain. The lamp flame bent, recovered, and drew light across a crown-shaped rim of dry rock. Beyond it, black water churned far below. I remembered riding ahead of the caravan at dusk. I remembered the storm whistle at the cave mouth, three falling notes that meant shelter or danger depending on which roadwarden had carved it. After that came a coldness at my boots, though I could not place where.

I asked, “How long was I senseless?”

“Less than an hour.”

“Where is my cousin?”

“Above us, I think. Someone is working a rope through the signal fissure.”

“Which way out?”

She pointed with an open hand. “The upper path. Flooded at the first bend. It should clear when the rain weakens.”

“Why can’t I remember?”

The queen glanced at the lamp. “The low air.”

I waited.

The attendant tied off the bandage and began counting without looking up. “Two dry blankets. Half a water jar. Salts. One sound lamp. Your left hand is cut.”

Only then did I see the blood dried between my fingers.

The queen said, “Cold, carbon-heavy air settles in the basin. We taste it before you do. It still slows us. Humans lose their feet, then their order of thought. Some wake without the last part.”

“You knew it was there.”

“Earlier than you. Not early enough.” She touched the bandage at her flank. “I went down when I heard your whistle.”

“That was your whistle.”

“No. Yours.”

My brass storm whistle hung from the snapped loop of my belt. I picked it up. A thread of black-green scale remained caught in the broken leather.

Somewhere above, stone rang twice. The attendant answered by striking the floor twice with the wooden handle of a spoon.

I raised my knife.

“Falling-stone warning,” the queen said. “Two taps. We have three drilled signals here: stop, move, and stone. Nothing else.”

The tapping came again, followed by a voice made thin by water and distance.

My cousin.

I lurched to my feet. The queen did not move to block me, but the ledge tilted under my boots. I planted one hand on the wall.

“That is the low air’s remainder,” she said.

“Or your medicine.”

“You have taken none.”

The attendant held up the stoppered jar, as if that ended the subject.

I found the signal fissure behind a curtain of runoff. It was a split in the wall scarcely wider than my shoulders. A rope rasped within it. The queen could not have forced her upper body through, much less the rest of her.

“I’ll go alone,” I said.

“Yes.”

I had expected an argument and mistrusted the absence of one. “You don’t want your prisoner back?”

“I want to keep you,” she said.

The words stopped me with one knee in the fissure.

The attendant shut the medicine case. The queen added, “Six days. Paid. You know surface warning marks, and ours failed to turn you from the basin. I require someone who can tell me why.”

“Keep me employed.”

“If you accept.”

“And if I don’t?”

“Leave when the upper path opens.”

No plea for trust. No smile. She settled lower while the attendant tucked the medicine case under a rock lip.

I crawled into the fissure.

The stone squeezed my shoulders and smelled of iron-rich mud. Three body lengths in, the passage bent. The queen called something after me—two ordinary words, perhaps *left wall*—but runoff struck the crack between us. Her consonants tore away. Only the drawn hiss of breath reached me.

Ahead, my cousin shouted my childhood kin-title.

“I’m here.”

The rope jerked against my wrist. I caught it.

“Tie in,” my cousin said. “We’ll pull you clear.”

A second voice cut across theirs. “Not over that lip. Knees down. No load yet.”

The rope carrier. I had seen them rig wagon teams on slopes where everyone else preferred prayer.

I crawled until I could see two blurred faces above a slant of water. The fissure opened beneath their shelf, its lower lip a chalky blade of stone.

“Did you see me fall?” I asked.

“I saw that thing take you.” My cousin reached down. “Give me your arm.”

“Before that. Did you see me in the basin?”

“You rode past the warning stakes.”

“Did you see me fall?”

“The bend hid you for half a minute. Then she had you wrapped from neck to boot. I know what I saw.”

“From up here?”

“Close enough. Come on.”

Behind me, the queen shouted. The fissure pared the words into a long sibilance. My cousin flinched and seized the rope.

The carrier said, “Wait. That edge is shedding.”

“They’re within reach.”

“No load.”

“Pull,” my cousin ordered me. “Now.”

I had one knee on the chalk lip when they hauled. The rope snapped tight under my arm. White stone broke with the sound of a plate struck against a table.

The fissure floor dropped.

I fell backward into the chamber in a burst of water and grit. The rope burned through my palm. I let it run, hit the crown ledge on one hip, and slid toward the black basin until the queen’s hand caught the back of my coat.

The crack widened above us. Runoff that had been threading down one wall poured through the new opening and cut a foaming channel across the ledge, between our shelf and the high side. Beside the wall, the attendant lost hold of the medicine case. The queen released my coat immediately, threw both arms around the attendant, and took the impact of falling stones along her wounded flank. Her body recoiled from the edge, carrying the attendant into a shallow alcove.

My cousin shouted, “She’s got you again!”

“She let go.” I spat grit. “Stop pulling.”

The rope carrier’s voice came sharper. “I had no load. You loaded it.”

“Help me get my kin out.”

“Then stop sawing the line over broken rock.”

The rope lay across the new channel, slapping in muddy water. Its free length still reached me. I dragged it off the crumbling lip and fed it around a basalt knob on my side.

“Pay me slack,” I called.

“Come up the line,” my cousin said.

“Slack. The ledge under them is going.”

The queen had braced her tail against the alcove wall. Blood ran fresh beneath her bandage. The attendant, one arm hanging close to the body, peered past her at the water.

“Shoulder,” the attendant said. “Mine. Not broken. Queen’s cloth is through. Two people above. One below standing badly.”

“I’m standing,” I said.

The attendant looked at my feet. I looked too. One boot was planted half in the channel, though I remembered setting it on dry stone.

The air had changed. The lamp flame near the floor was a small blue bead now. Cold climbed inside my trousers. Thoughts arrived like badly packed cargo: rope, cousin, queen, exit, and no certainty about which had to move first.

The queen tasted the air with a quick opening of her mouth. “The basin is being pressed upward.”

“Bad air rising?”

“Yes.”

“How long?”

“Not long.”

“How long?”

“I cannot measure it.” Her precision had shortened to its bones. “We climb now.”

The obvious way was the fissure. Its lip had just proved what it thought of us. I looked past the queen instead, following the route as I would judge a washed trail: where silt gathered, where water ran clear, where a crack stayed dry because air moved through it. High above the attendant’s alcove, a seam of grey showed between leaning slabs.

“That chimney,” I said. “Does it reach the mouth?”

“A hand’s width at the top,” the attendant said. “Enough air.”

“Enough for us,” the queen said. “The upper opening is wider behind the slab.”

My cousin called, “No. Take the rope here.”

“That lip won’t hold three loads.”

“You’re confused.”

“Yes,” I said. “And I’m still the outrider.”

The carrier leaned into view. “Chimney line looks cleaner. I need a second anchor.”

I pointed to a dark horn of stone above the fissure. “Back it with that.”

“Too sharp.”

“My saddle blanket’s by the hide. Folded double.”

My cousin began, “We are not rigging a rescue for—”

“Blanket,” the carrier said. “Now.”

The queen crossed the foaming cut first, not by clearing it but by filling its safe edge with her body. She locked the thick end of her tail around a rib of stone beside the alcove and reached across to the chimney slab. Her right hand found a seam. Her left arm curved behind the attendant’s back.

“Move,” she said.

The attendant answered with one tap of the spoon against stone: the drilled signal for movement. Then they slid along the inside of the queen’s braced body, one useful arm working, feet testing each hold. The queen took their weight when the ledge crumbled under a heel. Her wounded flank trembled.

I fed the padded rope across behind the attendant and passed it up. The carrier caught it, wrapped the sharp horn, and called the load each time they changed hands. My cousin obeyed for three breaths, then reached down for me.

“Come while she’s holding it.”

I put my foot into the cut and forgot where my other foot belonged.

The water seemed to split into two channels, then four. My cousin’s arm doubled above me. I blinked hard, but the chamber did not settle.

The queen said, “I can brace the break or carry you. Not both.”

“Then leave them,” my cousin said. “We have the line.”

“The line isn’t on me,” I said.

“I can put a loop down.”

The carrier said, “Not a blind waist loop on a confused climber.”

The attendant reached the first shelf in the chimney and wedged the medicine case behind their knees. “One injured above the cut,” they reported. “One dizzy below. Queen failing.”

The queen’s fingers slipped a joint along the seam.

I knew the reach across was less than two paces. I also knew I could no longer trust my knees to understand that.

“Coil me,” I said.

The queen looked down.

Fear went through me so cleanly that for a moment I could think again. I pointed, because the words mattered and I did not want more of them than necessary. “Once at my hips. Once below my shoulders. Leave this much at my ribs.” I held my hand sideways against my chest. “Across to the chimney. Put me down on the shelf.”

“Agreed.”

“And release when I say.”

“Yes.”

“You can’t stop bracing yet,” the carrier called. “Give me ten breaths.”

They threw a loop to my cousin, who caught it and cursed at the force. The carrier talked them through a body belay: feet against the rear wall, rope across the padded horn, no wrapping a wrist. My cousin tried to hurry; the carrier made them reset one sliding boot. I called the chimney holds. The queen shifted her brace when I called. Above, the carrier set the anchor and my cousin took the hauling side.

I clipped my belt ring to the line and crawled close to the queen. Her body moved around me, one measured band at my hips, another under my arms. The pressure stayed clear of the hand-width I had shown her.

When she shifted me against her side, something struck loose inside my head: floodwater white at the edge of lamplight, my fingers jammed through a copper arm band, my boots knocking empty rock. My own voice, hoarse and near her shoulder.

*Don’t drop me. Don’t—*

The rest vanished. I had that fragment and nothing around it. The voice was mine.

“I remember asking,” I said.

“Good,” my cousin answered too quickly. “Now come up.”

The queen did not answer at all. Her attention was on the carrier.

“Set,” the carrier called.

My cousin took the strain. The rope tightened from my belt to the horn, replacing some of the pull the queen’s tail had held. The attendant struck one tap. Move.

The queen unhooked her tail from the basalt knob.

For one breath we hung over the cut, the rope carrying part of me, her left hand on the chimney slab, her right arm clamped to a seam. Then her body drove forward. Water hit my boots. The fresh bandage at her flank split, and her next breath came as a dry click, but she crossed. She placed me on the shelf beside the medicine case.

“Release,” I said.

The coils opened before the last sound left my mouth. She kept one palm under my elbow until my weight was on stone, then removed it.

The carrier hauled. My cousin pulled in time rather than ahead of them. I crawled upward, pushing the medicine case while the attendant climbed one-handed before me. Below, the queen withdrew the final length of her tail just as the crown ledge broke and went into the basin.

She came last, using both arms and the pressure of her long body against opposite walls. Halfway up she stopped.

Two taps sounded beneath us.

Stone.

Nobody translated it into more. The attendant flattened. I jammed the medicine case under the shelf. My cousin held. The carrier locked the rope. A slab struck where the queen’s head had been; she folded sideways, waited for the smaller fragments to pass, and climbed again.

The air changed first. It lost the cold mineral weight. Then the chimney widened, and rain-grey light showed an upper mouth beyond a row of teethlike rocks. We crawled into fresh wind one by one.

The path outside had become a brown torrent, too deep to cross before morning. For the moment, the mouth was as far as rescue went.

The attendant made us sit by the outer wall and distributed the remaining water without discussion. The queen lay along the inner rock while the attendant cut away her ruined bandage. My cousin hovered over me, touching my shoulder every few breaths as though I might disappear between one glance and the next.

“We take you as soon as that drops,” they said.

“If it drops enough.”

“It will.”

The carrier inspected the rope’s abraded span. “Not by dawn, unless the rain stops now.”

“I wasn’t asking you.”

“I was answering the load.”

My cousin rounded on the queen. “You stay away from my kin.”

The queen’s face had gone still with pain. “They are free to sit where they choose.”

“You call wrapping them free?”

“I saw one carry,” the carrier said. They ran a thumb over a damaged strand. “Requested. Released at the shelf. I saw the queen hold the attendant when the ledge went. I did not see what happened below before we arrived.”

“You heard her say she wanted to keep them.”

“I heard half the sounds in that throat.”

My cousin looked at me. “You’re not taking this offer.”

The command landed where concern had been. I understood both and liked neither.

I asked the queen, “The six days. What pay?”

“Two silver weights per day. Meals. Surface work only once the path is safe.”

“Sleeping place?”

“The private niche beside this mouth.”

I looked. It was dry, human-sized, and completely open on one side.

“No door,” I said.

“There is no door.”

“I come to the mouth every day.”

“Yes.”

“Unrestricted. And when the upper path opens, I can leave before the six days are done.”

“Yes. You are paid for the days worked.”

“I’ll take the trial. One recovery night first.”

The attendant glanced at my bruised ribs. “Necessary.”

The queen said, “Accepted.”

My cousin swore under their breath. “She is dangerous.”

“Yes,” I said. Seven metres of injured muscle had just held up a broken route. I looked at the torrent outside. “So is that path.”

“That isn’t the same.”

“No.”

Nothing in the cave proved what had happened to travelers on other roads, or in other years. My cousin did not withdraw the accusation. The carrier did not offer the queen a clean character in exchange for one witnessed rescue. By the time the rain weakened, we had agreed only that nobody would attempt the outer path in darkness.

The attendant cleaned my palm, bound it, and sent me to the niche. I laid out my own bedroll there, with my pack and knife beside it. Across the mouth, my cousin argued quietly with the rope carrier about the morning anchors. Deeper in, the queen asked for the narrow bandage instead of the broad one, and the attendant told her there was no broad one left.

I set my boots where I could find them in the dark and slept until the attendant woke me to check my ribs.

stories.title: Held Together
stories.prompt: a Married hero couple going through a rough patch get captured by a married villain couple and are surprised at how healthy their relationship is.
stories.body:
# Held Together

At 2:13 in the morning, the transfer station's ventilation stopped, and Renata heard Jonas's patrol app reroute them.

"West stairs," its flat voice said. "Nearside remains with Fixedpoint."

Beyond the service doors, reserve batteries held enough charge to keep three neighborhood clinics and an assisted-living tower cool through the hottest night of the year. On Renata's phone, the station diagram showed a breaker fault in red and an access alarm in amber. The west stairs curled around two locked landings. The cable trench ahead was open, straight, and four metres across.

"The trench is faster," she said.

Jonas stood behind her on the concrete steps, broad shoulders blocking the emergency light. "The app says west."

"You wrote the app."

"I changed one permission."

"Mine."

Somewhere below, metal struck metal. The temperature display beside the door read forty-one degrees. A second access sensor turned amber.

"We can have this fight upstairs," Jonas said. "West stairs. Now."

Renata looked through the open gate at the landing beyond the trench. Four metres, clear line, no one visible. She went Nearside.

Space caught her behind the eyes. The landing replaced the step beneath her boots, and the world tipped left before righting itself. She kept one hand on the rail until the depth returned. First transit.

"Renata."

Ahead, through another open grille, the main-floor catwalk ran beside the reserve bus. Less than five metres. The shortest route had always been a chain of small, certain things.

She made the second transit before Jonas reached the trench.

This landing arrived doubled. Two yellow rails slid together, then apart. She blinked until they agreed on one position, but by then a woman in insulated work clothes had stepped within arm's reach of the lighting conduit.

The lights died from her outward.

Not a station-wide collapse. A moving absence, three metres across, following the woman as active circuits emptied into the two silver cells mounted on a low sled behind her. Brownout. Livia Kade turned her bare hand over, measuring the last blue thread of current across her palm.

"She's early," Livia said.

"Still on sequence," Xavier Kade answered from above.

Two amber tags flashed on the catwalk. The shutter behind Renata dropped so hard its bottom edge starred the concrete. A weighted baffle swung across the catwalk, its offset steel slats showing only other steel. Xavier, Downforce in the case files, stepped out on the overhead gantry with a battery harness tight against his ribs.

Renata turned toward the last place she had seen Jonas. No clear line remained.

A pale plane grew under the descending shutter, rigid and translucent. A second formed at the far edge of his six-metre sight, reaching toward the baffle. Jonas had committed both at once. For perhaps a second, Renata saw him between them: jaw set, hands spread, trying to make two paths exist where she had left him none.

Livia crossed close to the wall conduit. His comm light went black.

Xavier touched two fingers to his harness. The tagged shutter multiplied its downward load. Jonas's first plane bowed, not bending but sinking into cracked concrete as the floor failed beneath it. The second vanished when he pulled one numbed hand toward the manual latch. Too late. Another shutter sealed him into the relay bay.

The baffle struck Renata across the shoulder and drove her into a floor cage. A U-shaped anchor yoke closed over her ankles. Xavier planted a tag on it, and the steel became too heavy even to rock.

"That's three," Livia said.

"West shutter, relay shutter, anchor," Xavier said. "Sixty seconds."

The last slat locked into place. Every opening in Renata's cage faced a backing plate. She could see strips of floor, pieces of equipment, one of Jonas's boots six metres away. Nowhere she could go.

Above the bus, the red reserve clock changed from 45:00 to 44:59.

Livia pulled the first cell's leads toward the live cabinet. "Begin."

***

The Kades did not celebrate.

Livia positioned herself beside the active reserve circuit and let current vanish into the cell within her living field. Xavier checked the cage, the relay shutter, then the route to the loading ramp. He marked each task on a grease board clipped to the sled.

"Return before auxiliary," he said.

"After auxiliary." Livia watched a meter tremble. "If you close return first, the clinic feed sees the dip."

Xavier studied the switch labels, erased one arrow with his thumb, and drew it again beneath AUX. "After auxiliary."

"Yes."

No score kept. No little victory placed aside for later. Renata hated them more for how ordinary it looked.

She pulled against the anchor yoke. Its added load drove the cuff edges through her suit and into bone. Xavier glanced over.

"Don't," he said. "It won't get lighter because you're angry."

"The cooling wards lost twelve minutes last month," Renata said. "People in that tower can't sweat properly."

Livia's meter climbed. "They have room batteries."

"For forty minutes."

"Then your utility will have five minutes to transfer the reserve after we're gone."

"If your staged fault didn't damage the switchgear."

Livia looked at the scorched cabinet, then at the charging cell. "Xavier, temperature."

"Fifty-three."

She had heard Renata. She simply returned to the theft.

From the relay bay, Jonas said, "How many transits do you have?"

Renata found his face through two misaligned slots. "Work your latch."

"I need your remaining count."

"You don't need to authorize it."

"Not what I said."

"It was the shape of it."

He wrapped both hands around the manual lever. They did not close properly. Concurrent planes always numbed his fingers, beginning at the tips and moving inward. Renata had watched him fumble keys after patrol and teased him for refusing mittens in winter. Tonight the lever slipped from his palms.

"No more transits," he said. "Not until I can get you a line and support the landing."

There it was again. The shape and the substance.

Renata leaned back from the slots.

The first minute ended. Amber light faded from the anchor tag, and some of its crushing weight released. Xavier's harness fans spun up to cool the spent cycle. He tested the yoke with his boot before Renata could lift it, then renewed the downward load as soon as the tag answered.

Jonas had seen it too. "Sixty seconds," he said.

She gave him nothing.

At 31:18, Livia moved the intake leads from the first cell to the second. The first was the size of a carry-on case, finite and nearly full, its charge bars wavering orange. Xavier peeled the cooling west-shutter tag from its mount and braced it against the cell housing to reseat a clamp.

"Hold the tag against the housing," Livia said. "I'll pull the spike."

"No."

She looked up.

Xavier opened his hand. The center of his glove had blistered glossy over a burn. "The housing is over limit. Ceramic handle or it waits."

Livia checked the thermal strip. "Ceramic."

She fetched the handled clamp herself and set it within his reach. He seated it. She pulled the spike down into her field, and the cell steadied.

Xavier returned the tag to the west-shutter mount without engaging it.

"Abort at seventy-eight," Xavier said.

"Seventy-eight," she agreed.

The reserve clock continued to fall. Behind the far maintenance door, somebody struck twice, paused, then struck twice again. Utility workers. Alive, at least. The station display showed clinic demand rising with the outside temperature.

Renata waited for the anchor to cool, jammed her fingers beneath it, and heaved. One edge rose a centimetre. She twisted her right ankle. The doubled cuff became one too late; pain ran up her shin, and the yoke slammed down when Xavier renewed the tag.

"Stop testing it alone," Jonas said.

"Stop giving me orders through a wall."

"Then answer one question. How many?"

"Enough."

"That isn't a number."

She knew. That was why she had chosen it.

Livia crouched by the second cell. Its charge indicator jumped, fell, then blinked amber.

"You seated it wrong," she said.

Xavier did not turn from the loading ramp. "Seated at sixteen. Checked at twenty."

"It's moving now."

"Then something changed."

Livia put her hand beside the intake without touching it. Current made a fine blue web across her knuckles, and the station lights nearest her dimmed. She checked the reserve meter, then the cell.

"Bus sag," she said. A beat passed. "I read it as the clamp. That was mine."

Xavier came back. "Can you hold fifty percent?"

"Forty-six."

"Do that."

She caught his burned wrist before he reached for the clamp. "Open."

He opened his hand. Two fingers curled; the others shook.

"You don't renew the west shutter until your hand cools," she said.

"That leaves the ramp route open."

"I know what it leaves."

"All right."

She released him. He switched hands, and they returned to the cell without filling the silence.

Renata pressed her forehead to the cage steel. She had expected vanity, cruelty, one of them performing dominance for the other. What she saw was worse and smaller: correction accepted, limits believed, harm divided efficiently. They could do all of that and still watch the clinic demand climb.

At 12:06 remaining, Jonas said, "I can make one reliable plane. Two, and I won't have hands for the release."

Not a command. An inventory.

Renata looked through the lowest slot. Xavier's anchor tag would gray at the end of its minute. Each time it did, his harness fan ran while he checked the sled wheels. To move the charged cells up the ramp, he would need the sled loaded downward for traction against the vibrating floor. Three tags, no fourth. He had rehearsed the transfer twice with his eyes.

"One," she said.

Jonas went still.

"I used two after 1:31. One left in the six-hour window." She swallowed. The cage seemed to lean toward her. "After the concussion, the second makes edges split. The third takes depth. Last time, seventeen minutes. I couldn't tell the floor from a step."

"Last time?"

"Three weeks ago."

His breath left him through his nose. She waited for the contingency tree: dates, reporting failures, the predictable list of all the ways she had made them unsafe.

"What can you see now?" he asked.

"The near slat. Your boot when you move it. Not their faces unless they cross the middle gap."

"All right."

The words sounded unfinished in his mouth.

Renata gripped the yoke. "Tell me what you've seen."

"Baffle pivots toward me when the anchor tag cools. Hinge opening is five point six metres from my left slot. His transfer takes four seconds. The sled crosses your middle gap after the tag seats."

"Can your plane hold the baffle?"

"Thirty seconds."

He waited.

Renata measured the strip of concrete beyond the middle gap. Four metres, perhaps four and a half. It doubled if she stared too hard, but both versions were inside her limit.

"On the next transfer," she said. "Wedge the baffle. I lift the yoke when the load drops. I go to the clear patch by the sled."

"You'll land blind."

"Nearly. You'll route me to your release."

His boot shifted into view, then stopped. "Yes."

***

At 8:41, the anchor tag went gray.

Renata lifted. The yoke came off the floor, ordinary steel again, heavy but possible. Jonas's pale plane grew through the left slot, a single rigid sheet expanding into the baffle hinge. Metal screamed. The offset slats opened three centimetres, then ten.

Xavier looked over. His burned hand hovered near the tag.

"Sled first," Livia said. "We're below exit traction."

He tore the amber marker from Renata's yoke and slapped it onto the sled frame. The cells sank against their suspension. Their weight bit the wheels into the ramp.

The middle gap cleared.

Renata chose the patch of floor she could see and went.

The cage vanished. Concrete struck both boots at once. Then the room lost its distances.

Rails floated near and far. Livia became two dark figures beside a blue flare. Renata dropped to one knee before the false floor could move under her. Her stomach surged. Third transit. None left until after 7:31.

"Forward two paces," Jonas called. His command voice caught on the first word, then changed. "Your pace. Handrail at your right knee."

Renata found the rail by sweeping her hand. Behind her, Xavier hauled at the loaded sled. Livia left the bus to intercept, and the charge stream broke as soon as the active circuit passed beyond her three-metre field.

"One pace," Jonas said. "Relay release is shoulder height. Orange handle. Twenty centimetres left."

There were three orange blurs. Renata closed one eye. Two remained.

"Which one?"

Silence, just long enough for him to look instead of assume. "Farther left. Your hand is below it. Up."

Her fingers struck the handle. She pulled.

The relay shutter lifted. Jonas ducked under it as Xavier renewed the tag, and the metal crashed onto the plane Jonas formed beneath it. One plane. His right hand hung half closed.

"Main isolation?" Renata asked.

"Six paces behind you. Yellow wheel."

Livia moved back toward the bus, choosing the cells over Renata. Current flared again. Xavier abandoned the sled and came toward Jonas, one tag control in his good hand.

They countered on different instincts and blocked each other's route.

"Xavier," Livia said. "West rail is seventy-two."

"Sled or shutter?"

"Sled. Give me the route."

He stepped back at once and dragged the sled sideways, clearing her path to the live cabinet. "Two metres. Clamp high. Then ramp."

Jonas could have put a second plane across them. Renata saw his shoulders set for it, saw his numb fingers twitch.

"One wall," she said.

He kept the shutter off them.

"Wheel is five paces now," he said. "Drift right."

Renata moved through the swimming geometry. At the yellow blur, she used both hands until she found the rim. It resisted, then turned. The reserve bus separated with a blow she felt in her teeth. Clinic demand disappeared from Livia's intake meter, isolated behind the mechanical switch.

The cells remained charged. Their rig whined against the cut circuit, hunting for a path.

"Ground bar," Jonas said. "Low left."

"I can't find low."

"Stop."

She stopped.

"Your left boot is touching the housing. Bar is on the housing. Slide your heel back."

Metal knocked her boot. Renata crouched without trusting the floor and closed both hands around the insulated grip.

Livia saw what she held. "Don't."

The plea was for the cells, not the reserve or the workers behind the door.

Renata pulled the station's emergency ground into place.

The siphon load went down the copper braid. Both cells flashed white. Livia broke her field and stumbled away from the cabinet. Xavier caught the back of her harness, keeping her clear of the arcing leads without touching them.

"Seventy-six," she said.

"Ramp is open."

"Seventy-seven."

Xavier reached for the sled, burned hand failing around its handle. The cell casing ticked as it expanded.

"Seventy-eight," Livia said.

He let go.

Together they backed toward the service ramp, Xavier counting the steps twice when smoke hid the edge. Livia cut power from one active door circuit as she passed within range; the lock released dead rather than opening for them. Xavier shouldered it wide. He tapped the still-mounted west-shutter tag, increased the shutter's downward load, and followed her through before the cooling harness could answer again.

Jonas's plane expired. The shutter hit concrete between the heroes and the ramp.

He did not make another.

"Pursuit?" he asked.

Renata listened to the pounding behind the maintenance door. One worker's strikes had become uneven.

"No. Staff first."

"Yes."

They grounded the cells, released the damaged switchgear from the reserve, and opened the maintenance room by hand. One technician had a bleeding scalp. The other lay beside a fallen tool cabinet with an ankle swelling inside her boot. Jonas formed a single plane as a rigid litter while Renata, moving by touch and his plain directions, kept the technician level. They carried her to the cooler stairwell and waited for responders instead of the Kades.

At 3:28, exactly seventy-five minutes after the ventilation had stopped, a hospital physician shone a narrow light across Renata's eyes.

"Tell me every transit in the last six hours," she said.

Renata sat on an intake bed with a basin between her shoes. Jonas stood by the curtain, his hands wrapped in warming pads. A patrol supervisor waited on speakerphone beside the blood-pressure cuff.

"Three," Renata said. "Two before capture, one to escape. The window started at 1:31. I had a concussion last month. Since then the second transit doubles edges, and the third removes usable depth. I hid the change from medical and from my partner."

The physician recorded it without looking at Jonas. "Observation until the depth loss clears. You agree?"

"Yes."

On the phone, the supervisor asked, "Why did your route split?"

Jonas shifted a warming pad from one palm to the other. "I added a field veto to our patrol app. I did it unilaterally, and I didn't disclose it to command. Renata rejected the route. We stopped sharing information before entry."

He did not add a reason after the fact.

Renata looked toward him and found two Jonases at the curtain.

"Remove the veto," she said.

"Now?"

"Now. Leave the route log intact for review."

"Okay." His fingers would not work the phone. "Will you unlock it for me?"

She did. He talked her through the settings but did not touch her hand. The permission changed from PARTNER OVERRIDE to SHARED CONFIRMATION.

The physician rolled a visual-field target to the end of the bed. "Do you want him in the room for the assessment?"

Renata considered the two blurred figures, the marriage she still inhabited and the field partnership she could not decide from a hospital bed.

"For the assessment, yes."

Jonas looked at the empty spaces on either side of her. "Left or right?"

"Left."

He moved there and waited while the physician raised the first light.

stories.title: Not Friday
stories.prompt: “Bro just trust me! She likes you!” “you said that about the last 4 girls an-” “shut up! I wasn't wrong about the last four. They didn't leave cause you misinterpreted signals. They left cause you waited 6+ months to be a man. Now ask her out before she gets tired of you!” “……ok i am going for it!”
stories.body:
# Not Friday

Wesley had carried eight folding chairs at once exactly one time. He had the scars on two knuckles and the dent in the arts center's baseboard to prove it. On Wednesday afternoon he carried four, which left Jamar Ellis two free hands for opinions.

"Bro, just trust me. She likes you."

Jamar walked backward between the chair stacks, steering by confidence. Behind him, forty-eight black seats waited to become eight straight rows in the rehearsal hall. Wesley set down his load before Jamar could hit one.

"You said that about the last four women, and—"

"Shut up. I wasn't wrong about the last four." Jamar planted both palms on the chair backs as if calling a witness. "They didn't leave because you misread some mysterious signal. They left because you waited six-plus months to find out anything. Now ask Beatriz before she gets tired of waiting for you to ask."

"Or she isn't waiting."

"Six-plus months," Jamar repeated, having selected the useful portion of Wesley's sentence. "Each time. Pattern established."

"Not each time."

"Objection."

"Nobody invited you to court."

"The court convened when you made the same mistake four times."

They had known each other long enough that Wesley could hear the concern inside the performance. Jamar hated watching him retreat into maybe. He hated it with the personal offense of a friend who had listened to every careful postmortem and believed most postmortems could have been replaced by one timely question.

That did not make him an authority on Beatriz Soto.

Wesley took a tape measure from his pocket. "Thirty-two inches between rows."

"Flight from evidence."

"Fire code."

They pulled the first row into place. The chair feet rasped against the old wood in brief, ugly bursts. Outside the hall, somebody tested the lobby lights, turning the open doorway amber and then white and then amber again.

"All right," Jamar said. "Exhibit one. Ceramics class. She asked if coffee would be a date. You said you needed to check your schedule."

"I did need to check it."

"For seven months?"

Wesley nudged a chair leg onto the tape mark. She had asked clearly. He had liked her, and the clarity had somehow given him more to lose. By the time he returned with an answer, she no longer wanted one.

Jamar raised a finger. "Exhibit two. You two kept talking about dinner, you kept improving the plan, she moved away."

"That was four months. And she moved for a job."

"Sustained as to four months."

The third woman had answered his eventual question with friendship, plainly and without cruelty. They had suffered one awkward volunteer shift and then been fine. This fact ought to have encouraged him. Instead, Wesley's mind had filed the awkward shift under preventable hazards and misplaced the rest.

The fourth had started seeing somebody else while Wesley waited for a level of certainty no other person could possibly supply. Jamar presented that history with two fingers raised, then four, then a broad gesture that nearly took out a chair.

"Those are four different situations," Wesley said.

"Four situations. One delay."

"The move wasn't caused by me. The friendship wasn't a failure. And the fourth met somebody. She didn't do that to make a point at me."

"Great. Excellent distinctions." Jamar shoved the next chair into line. "Ask on behalf of all your distinctions."

Wesley measured the aisle. He could name what Jamar was getting wrong. Beatriz's habit of saving him a dumpling during late setups did not reserve anything beyond a dumpling. The time she had texted him a picture of a display label with its apostrophe corrected proved she knew what irritated him, not what she wanted from him. She laughed at Jamar, too. She had given both of them rides when the buses stopped running. Friendly was not a coded contract.

Still, the four histories had one narrow piece of evidence in common. Waiting protected Wesley from answers while he called the protection consideration.

He folded the tape measure closed. "Okay. I'm going for it."

Jamar slapped the back of a chair instead of Wesley, which was why they remained friends. "Motion carries."

"You are not coming within twenty feet of the conversation."

"Unreasonable restriction."

"Thirty feet."

"I'll be in another room."

"Thank you."

"With excellent hearing."

The side door opened before Wesley could revise the terms. Beatriz came through hip-first, a cardboard file box balanced against one hip and a coil of blue cable hooked over her other arm. Her dark hair was pinned up with a pencil. Three revised run sheets stuck out of the box like surrender flags.

"One of you has hands," she said. "Possibly both."

Wesley took the box. Jamar accepted the cable and made a dignified show of not looking at him.

Beatriz put the run sheets on the front row. "The Friday check-in volunteer canceled. The replacement says maybe, which is no. I moved the student quintet ahead of the auction, the food delivery window is now five-fifteen to five-forty, and the upstairs storage lock is sticking again."

"How was the contract orientation?" Wesley asked.

"Three hours about ladders. My first paid call is Saturday morning, assuming Friday doesn't bury me under a silent auction basket."

"We can take check-in," Jamar said.

"I can," Wesley said at the same time.

Beatriz looked between them. "Wesley on the desk. He knows the ticket sheet. Jamar, float between lobby and house. No improvising new donation tiers."

"That happened once."

"It happened on three signs."

Jamar carried the cable toward the stage, shaking his head at this hostile account of his service. As he passed Wesley, he lifted his eyebrows twice. Wesley concentrated on the file box until the eyebrows had safely left his peripheral vision.

For the next hour, Beatriz had half a conversation with everyone. She marked chair positions in blue tape, found the missing key in the wrong envelope, took a call from the food vendor, and corrected the same start time on twelve programs. Wesley watched any plan involving a dramatic Friday confession become obviously absurd. Friday belonged to the showcase. It also stood between Beatriz and a new job she had spent months trying to get. Adding his uncertainty to her load would not make the question more romantic.

It did leave him Wednesday.

At six-twenty, Beatriz checked the bus app and began packing her papers. Wesley had rehearsed seven openings. Two required a transition no real conversation would ever provide. One sounded like a calendar invitation composed during a fire. In another, he explained so carefully that she was free to decline that the invitation almost disappeared.

He carried the file box with her through the lobby. The front doors stood open to the mild evening, and buses sighed at the curb beyond the plaza. People crossed between them with grocery bags and backpacks. If Beatriz wanted to leave, leaving was already happening all around her.

"I can take that from here," she said, reaching for the box.

Wesley gave it to her. His best opening vanished. Then the second-best.

"Could I—" He stopped. The rest of that opening had already become an explanation.

"Would you like to have dinner with me after the showcase on Friday?" he said. "Just the two of us. If you don't, that's okay. I won't make Friday weird."

Beatriz settled the box against her hip. For two seconds she looked only tired, and Wesley's mind tried to build exits for both of them.

"I am interested," she said. "But don't backfill every friendly thing I did into a promise. I hadn't made one."

"I know. Or I was trying to know that."

"Those are different."

"Yes."

The bus rounded the corner, its route number bright in the dusk. Beatriz shifted the box again.

"And not Friday," she said. "Friday is the showcase. Saturday is my first contract call, and I will still be thinking in cables until at least Monday. Tuesday at seven. The noodle place beside the library."

The bus hissed to a stop.

"Tuesday works," Wesley said.

"Good. Send me your order if the food vendor texts you back."

She climbed aboard with the file box. Wesley stood on the plaza until he remembered that staying there would not make the answer more answered. Then he went inside and sent her the vendor's revised count.

* * *

Friday began by subtracting people.

At four-fifty-two, the replacement check-in volunteer sent a message containing the words *so sorry* and a photograph of a flat tire. At five-ten, the student quintet arrived with five students and one additional cello. At five-twenty, one of the two card readers refused to recognize the building's network.

Wesley sat behind the lobby table with a cash box, a printed guest list, and Jamar leaning over his shoulder.

"She assigned you to the money," Jamar said quietly. "Trust. Significant."

"She assigned me because you invented platinum-level raffle tickets last time."

"Community enthusiasm punished again."

"Put the programs on the left."

Jamar put the programs on the left. For nearly six minutes, he spoke only about programs.

By six-thirty the lobby had filled with damp coats and the smell of baked cheese from the warming trays. Beatriz moved through it with a headset over one ear, counting lanyards and answering questions in pieces.

"Two vegetarian trays downstairs," a volunteer told her.

"Bring one up now. Leave one sealed."

"The quintet wants six chairs."

"Five players, six chairs. Fine. No seventh."

She reached Wesley's table and set down a roll of drink tickets. "How many checked in?"

"Eighty-three. Eleven prepaid haven't arrived. The card reader on the right is dead, but the left one is keeping up."

"Cash?"

"Balanced at two hundred forty."

"Good. East doors open at six-forty-five."

Jamar watched her go. "She said good to you differently."

Wesley handed him half the programs. "East doors."

The doors opened. The audience moved inside. At six-fifty-eight, two minutes before the welcome, every speaker in the black-box theater made a low electrical thump and fell silent.

For a moment the room absorbed the failure without understanding it. A hundred conversations continued under the work lights. Then the sound technician appeared at the lobby door, one hand pressed to his headphones, and beckoned so sharply that Beatriz was already moving before Wesley saw him.

She came back thirty seconds later.

"Main cable failed. Wesley, studio B upstairs. Orange road case. Bring two twenty-five-foot XLRs to the booth, then come back to the east doors. Don't wait backstage. Jamar, keep this aisle clear."

Wesley's mind supplied questions. Was the road case labeled on two sides or one? If the storage lock stuck, should he find the facilities volunteer or come back? Did two cables mean two loose or a joined pair? The questions queued neatly, each offering a small delay.

"Orange case. Two XLRs. Booth, then east doors," he repeated.

"Yes. Go."

He went.

The upstairs hall was dark except for the red glow of an exit sign. The storage lock resisted once, then opened when Wesley lifted the door by its handle. The orange case sat behind two rolling costume racks. He moved them, found the cables, and ran them down the back stairs without stopping to imagine what Beatriz might infer from his speed.

At the booth she took one cable from him without looking away from the technician. "Other one under the stage lip. Then doors."

Wesley passed it down, returned to the lobby, and stayed there. He explained the delay to late arrivals, found a chair for an older guest, and redirected three people who mistook the silent auction room for the theater. Through the wall came a burst of static, a voice saying *check*, and then applause when the voice came through clean.

The welcome began nineteen minutes late.

Jamar drifted back at seven-thirty with empty program boxes nested under his arm. "You notice she called you specifically."

"I notice you have nothing to do."

"I have pattern recognition."

"Take the empty trays downstairs."

"That's not my assigned—"

"Please."

Jamar studied him, perhaps hearing the edge that Wesley had not meant to add. Then he took the trays. "All right. Basement kitchen?"

"Service stairs are faster."

"See? A useful conversation."

At eight-forty, Beatriz appeared with her headset hanging around her neck. The welcome delay had spread. One performer had used the full original time, the auction had started late, and the closing quintet still needed a twelve-minute changeover. Wesley knew it was Beatriz's favorite act because she had attended two of their rehearsals and once made Jamar stand perfectly still in the lobby to hear the cello through the wall.

She placed both hands on the check-in table. "Numbers. How many people still here?"

Wesley checked the clicker and the departure marks. "One hundred twelve inside. Eight have left. Forty-two said they're taking the nine-forty bus, but some came in groups."

"Any bidders in the gallery now?"

He looked through the open doors. "Six. Two are filling out sheets."

"Facilities confirm ten o'clock hard close?"

"I asked when the sound went down. Alarm arms at ten-ten. They need the room empty at ten."

Beatriz tapped the table once. The quintet could have its full set or the event could have its promised ending time. Wesley wanted to tell her that cutting her favorite was unfair, that everybody would understand, that he could help somehow. None of those sentences changed the clock.

"Do you need another count?" he asked.

"No. Close the gallery at nine-fifteen. Last bids at nine-ten. Tell the quintet eight minutes, no encore. I'll apologize to them."

"Okay."

"And put the bus people on the aisle when they come out of the auction."

Wesley wrote the new times on the lobby board. He found the quintet's volunteer liaison and gave her the eight-minute limit. When the silent auction closed, he collected the pencils, directed the bus riders, and did not go backstage to see whether Beatriz was angry or disappointed or impressed. None of it would help her empty the room by ten.

The quintet played for eight minutes. Their final note was still moving through the room when Beatriz stepped out to thank the donors. The audience reached the lobby at nine-twenty-eight. The bus group left together. At nine-fifty-six, Wesley folded the last chair while Jamar rolled tape into a gray, useless ball.

Beatriz crossed the empty hall carrying a crate of bidder sheets.

"Table goes in the office," she told Wesley. "Chairs in stacks of six, not eight."

"A lesson I remember."

"Good. Tuesday, seven."

"Tuesday, seven."

She kept walking toward the office. Jamar opened his mouth.

Wesley pointed at the gray ball in his hand. "Trash."

Jamar considered an appeal, then dropped it into the bin.

* * *

On Tuesday evening, Wesley reached the noodle place at six-fifty-two without sending anyone a screenshot of the menu. He had looked at it twice, which was restraint by his standards.

Beatriz was already at a small table near the window. The pencil was gone from her hair. A strip of black stage tape clung to the cuff of her jacket, and there were shadows under her eyes that the restaurant's yellow lights did nothing to hide.

"You look tired," Wesley said, then wished he had chosen one of the other six openings available to him.

"I am tired. First contract weekend." She peeled the tape from her cuff and wound it around one finger. "I carried a fake brick wall up two flights because someone measured the freight elevator emotionally."

Wesley sat across from her. "Did the wall fit on the stairs?"

"After we removed a door. The door was real and heavier than the wall."

A server set down two menus and asked whether they wanted tea.

"Hot," Beatriz said. "Big pot."

Wesley nodded. "Please."

When the server left, Beatriz opened the menu and looked at him over its top edge. "Do you share appetizers, or do you become territorial?"

"Depends on the appetizer."

"Cucumber salad."

"Shareable."

"Scallion pancake?"

He pretended to require calculation. "Border dispute likely."

"We'll get two."

She marked the paper order slip. Wesley watched her choose the noodle thickness without consulting him, then slide the pencil across the table so he could choose his own. Outside, a bus pulled away from the curb. Beatriz asked what he did when the arts center did not need its chairs counted, and waited through his first, overly detailed answer until he found the part she had actually asked about.

The tea arrived. Then the cucumber salad, cold and sharp with vinegar, and two separate plates of scallion pancake.

stories.title: By Wing and Welcome
stories.prompt: After your kid daughter nurses a bat back to health, a strange looking couple show up on your doorstep, asking to be her god parents, claiming said bat was their son
stories.body:
# By Wing and Welcome

At seven thirteen, twelve evenings after Pippa found the bat on our doormat, she read his weight aloud while I held him in my gloved hands.

“Nine point two grams.”

“Check the decimal.”

My daughter bent until her braid brushed the scale. “Twelve point nine. I knew that. The six looks like a decimal when the light catches it.”

“It was a nine.”

“Then the nine looks like a six.” She wrote the correct number in the care log and underlined it once. Pippa was eleven and had spent twelve days learning that supervised wildlife care meant she recorded weights, changed water, counted mealworms, and kept the flight room quiet. It did not mean she got to put bare hands on a bat because she loved him.

The bat tucked his narrow head against my thumb. His right forearm had been cracked when Pippa found him, the wing dragging wet across the front step. That evening the joint moved cleanly and the membrane had healed to a thin pink seam. I lowered him to the landing board.

“May I check the other side?” I asked.

He put one claw on the green YES square.

Pippa and I had made the board on his third day, after he had ignored a dish I moved within reach, crossed half the recovery box, and planted himself on the word WATER. It offered YES, NO, STOP, WATER, PAIN, ALONE, and an alphabet strip—nothing more. A bat should not have been able to read block capitals. By then, a bat should not have been able to glare at my thermometer either. I had stopped saying should in front of him.

I examined the wing, then backed away. He climbed to the perch and shook himself. His ears flicked toward the rain ticking on the high window.

“Three full circuits tonight,” Pippa said. “Maybe four.”

“Three, if he chooses. Outdoor release is off while that storm sits over us.”

“I know. Controlled test.” She drew a box for the result. Beside it she had already written *door shut, fan off, water left* in her cramped capitals.

The doorbell rang.

The bat dropped flat against the perch. Pippa looked at me, then at the clock. Nobody visited on a release night, and nobody sensible visited in that weather without calling first.

“Stay here,” I said.

“You can't supervise me from the front door.”

She was right, which was irritating. I settled the bat in his open recovery box, carried it to the front hall, and had Pippa wheel the landing-board cart behind us. I kept my gloves on.

The couple outside looked as though the storm had discovered two people who had dressed for the wrong century. The woman's coat fastened diagonally with dozens of dull horn toggles. The thin edges of her ears rose through her soaked hair and turned separately, one toward my voice, one toward the recovery box. Beside her, a tall man wore a waxed coat cut with deep triangular pleats under the arms. Before he spoke, the skin at his throat tightened in two quick pulses.

“Is he there?” the woman asked.

The man said, “We believe the injured person in your care is our son, Teyo. He is twelve years old.”

The woman looked past my elbow, though she did not step closer. “And we came to ask if we may be godparents to your daughter.”

Pippa whispered, “They led with the second-weirdest part.”

I put my foot against the door. “Names. Yours, not his again.”

“Olya,” said the woman.

“Corven.” The man wiped rain from his mouth. “We understand that the combined request lacks an adequate sequence. Recovery first. Verification second. The pledge—if welcome—last.”

“Nothing is welcome yet,” I said. “How do you know there's a bat here?”

Olya's ears tipped toward the box. “I hear him.”

“You hear a bat.”

“I hear a frightened young one trying not to answer me.” Her hands closed on each other. “That isn't proof. I know.”

Corven gave me the date Teyo had disappeared. Twelve days ago. He described a healed notch along the left ear and an injury to the right forearm, neither of which they could see from the step. Then he said, “When he is upset in this body, he bites cloth hems but leaves the seams intact.”

Pippa opened the log without being told. Day four: *pulled towel under perch, three tooth marks, didn't rip it.* Day eight: *did it again after weighing.*

“People can guess,” I said.

“Not that,” Pippa said. “But they could've watched us.”

The lights went out.

For a moment the only illumination came from my battery alarm panel and the white tear of lightning above the road. Rain hammered the porch roof. In the recovery box, claws scraped cardboard.

I shut the door on the weather and locked it. That admitted Olya and Corven only as far as the tiled vestibule. “Pippa, backup pad.”

She was already kneeling at the cart. The small heat pad switched to its battery with an amber light. Its display settled on forty-eight minutes.

“Flight room will cool faster than the house,” I said. “We do this narrowly. You two stay here until he answers.”

Olya pressed both palms to her coat. Corven began, “Our kin can execute a voluntary bodily transition no more than once in the interval commencing at sunset and terminating at the subsequent sunset—”

“How long?”

“Three uninterrupted minutes without light. The change spends heat. It retains injury, hunger, memory, and the person.”

“Can you trigger it?”

“No name, touch, order, threat, appeal, or emotional extremity can initiate it in another person.”

“Plainly,” Pippa said.

Corven looked at her. Rainwater ran off his wing-cut sleeves. “No. We can't make him.”

“Can he stop once he starts?” I asked.

“Not safely that we know.”

“Then we don't start cold.” I checked the room thermometer: nineteen degrees and falling. “Twelve point nine grams. Healing forearm. He has flown only in this room, and not tonight. You will tell me only what affects his immediate safety.”

“Warm, awake, free to move,” Corven said. “And willing.”

Pippa rolled the cart into the flight room. I carried the open box. Olya and Corven waited behind the yellow tape I used to mark the handling area. The exterior release hatch was shut against the storm, but the door to the hall stayed open behind them.

The bat climbed out on his own. He ignored the board and stared at Olya.

She made a sound too high for me to hear. I knew only because her throat moved and the bat answered with a burst that my detector rendered as a scatter of descending clicks. He launched, circled once, and caught the mesh wall closest to her. Olya lifted a hand, then stopped it at her own chest.

Pippa watched the detector. “That's his found-something sound. Not yes. Just—I don't know. Excited.”

“Teyo,” Olya said. “Little—”

The bat dropped to the board and struck STOP.

Olya went silent so abruptly I heard the battery pad's relay click.

Corven took one step back. Then another.

I moved the board closer without touching the bat. “Do you want the two people from the door inside this room if they stay behind the tape and do not touch you?”

YES.

“Do you want Pippa and me to stay?”

YES.

“One question at a time,” Pippa told Corven. “He can spell, but it's slow, and his right side gets tired.”

Corven nodded as if she had given him a difficult professional instruction. “Understood.”

I pointed to the alphabet strip. “Are the letters T-E-Y-O your name?”

The bat tapped YES.

“Are Olya and Corven your parents?”

He held still long enough that Olya's breath caught. Then he crossed to YES.

Olya made no move toward him. She only crouched behind the tape and turned her face slightly away, giving him the side view rather than the full attention of her large, light-catching eyes.

“Did you leave their home on purpose?” I asked.

YES.

“Did you have permission?”

NO.

Corven closed his eyes. Olya whispered something I did not understand.

“Don't do that,” Pippa said.

Olya looked up.

“Not the other language. The sad noise like you already know everything. He hates when I do the sad voice.”

“Pippa,” I said.

“He does. Day six, after he wouldn't eat.”

Olya's fingers opened. “Thank you. I was answering for him with my face.” She tried the sentence again and lost it halfway. “I am afraid, so I keep—I see him and my hands—” She tucked them under her arms. “I will wait.”

The room thermometer showed eighteen. The pad read thirty-nine minutes.

“Do you want to change to the body that can speak?” I asked the bat.

YES.

“Now?”

YES.

“Are you in more pain than before the visitors came?”

NO.

He moved from NO to WATER.

“See?” Pippa said. “One thing.”

I set down the shallow dish. He drank, one wing slightly lifted for balance. Olya watched his ears instead of the dish.

“He dislikes moving air over his back when he is cold,” she said. “At home he crawls into the sleeve of my oldest coat. The brown one. It smells of cedar and burnt sugar.”

Pippa checked the log. “He hides under the towel when the vent comes on.”

“May I put this near him?” Olya opened her coat, revealing a lining patched in three shades of brown. “Not over him. He can enter or not.”

I asked. The bat selected YES.

Olya slid the coat across the floor and withdrew her hands before it crossed the tape. Pippa positioned it beside the landing board after he agreed to that too. He crawled halfway into one sleeve, nose working. His detector trace sprang into tight, rapid curves.

“Recognition,” Pippa said. “Maybe happy. You still have to ask.”

Olya nodded, but tears had reached her chin and she seemed unable to find any more words.

We prepared the room around his choices. I filled two sealed bottles from the hot-water tank while it still held heat and wrapped them in towels. Corven checked the blackout blind only when I told him he might. Pippa covered the alarm display with a folded cloth. When Corven suggested the recovery carrier, the bat struck NO before I finished the question.

“No carrier,” I said.

“The carrier would reduce the chance of a fall during altered balance,” Corven began.

The bat hit STOP.

Corven pressed his lips together.

I opened the carrier door and laid it on its side, available and empty. “He stays unrestrained.”

“Yes,” Corven said. This time there was no definition attached.

The pad showed twenty-seven minutes. We could wait for the power, but not with any assurance, and release into hard rain was no option. I wanted a veterinarian, a generator, daylight, and a week to decide whether impossible visitors were trustworthy. What I had was a cold animal who had just told me he was a child, two parents making themselves obey a strip of yellow tape, and Pippa noticing every time an adult let fear turn into permission they had never received.

“Who stays in the room?” I asked.

Through separate yes-or-no questions, Teyo chose all four of us. He wanted Olya and Corven behind the tape. He wanted Pippa beside me. He wanted no one touching him. He wanted the coat within reach and the carrier open. When I asked if we could bring up low light after three minutes, he chose YES.

“Last chance to stop before we start,” I said.

He rested one claw on YES.

Pippa corrected me. “That sounds like yes means stop.”

She was right again. I breathed out. “Do you still choose to change now?”

YES.

I shut the hall door, pulled the blind, and switched off my torch. The darkness was complete.

Pippa started the three-minute timer under the folded cloth. Nobody spoke. At first I heard the tiny working sounds of a bat inside fabric. Then the coat lining dragged across the floor. A heel struck the empty carrier and shoved it into the wall. Olya inhaled sharply but did not cross the tape. Somewhere in the second minute, the sounds became human breathing: quick, chilled, trying not to complain.

The timer vibrated against Pippa's palm.

“Teyo?” I said. “May I bring up the covered lamp?”

A boy's voice answered from the floor. “Yes. Low.”

I uncovered the lamp one fold at a time.

He was twelve, or near enough that the number fit his narrow shoulders and furious embarrassment. Olya's coat covered him from collarbone to shin. His ears were smaller than hers but had the same fine mobile tips; his eyes caught bronze at the edges. His right forearm lay guarded against his ribs. A thin healing abrasion crossed the inside of the wrist exactly where the wing seam had been.

Olya stayed behind the tape. “May I come to you?”

“Not yet.”

She sat down where she was.

I knelt outside his reach. “May I examine your arm?”

“In a minute. Bottle first.”

I rolled him one of the wrapped hot-water bottles. He trapped it between his knees. Pippa handed over the cup only after he asked. He drank, shivering hard enough to tap his teeth on the rim.

“Pippa said you could read,” I said.

“I can. Spelling with one foot is awful.”

“You used your left,” Pippa said.

“My right hurt.”

“I put the letters closer on that side.”

“You put Q beside P.”

Pippa turned to me. “That was one time.”

The ordinary irritation in his voice did more than his ears or Olya's coat had done. This was the same particular patient who shoved cards aside when they inconvenienced him.

He let me examine the arm. The change had not repaired it or broken it anew. The same forearm remained tender; the same motion caused him to flinch. His temperature worried me more. I wrapped a second warmed towel around his shoulders with his permission.

“Tell me who they are, and how you reached our door,” I said.

Teyo looked at his parents, then at Pippa. “Olya's my mother. Corven's my father. I left through my bedroom window. They said I wasn't cleared to fly alone after dark. I went anyway. There were moths by the school field. I followed them too far, hit a wire over your lane, and came down on the step.”

“Why our step?” Pippa asked.

“It was the first dry one. Then you came outside in socks and asked before you put the box over me.”

Pippa looked down at her slippers.

“Did you know your parents were searching?” I asked.

“I heard calls on three nights. I couldn't answer far enough after the fall. When I got stronger, I didn't change because it would take heat and I didn't know where I was. After that I wanted to finish the wing test.”

“You could've spelled HOME,” Pippa said.

“I didn't want them called until I knew I could fly.”

“That's not a good reason.”

“No.” Teyo looked at his parents. “It wasn't.”

“You wanted release?”

“I wanted to know if I could fly.” He glanced at Corven. “Before the lecture.”

Corven said, “There will be—” and stopped. “Yes. Later.”

“Do you want to go home with them tonight?” I asked.

Teyo drew the bottle closer. “Yes. I want you to check the arm first, and I want food. Then home. Medical care tomorrow. They can be angry after I eat.”

Olya laughed once, badly, and covered her mouth. “May I?”

Teyo considered her open arms. “You can sit here. Don't squeeze my right side.”

She crossed the tape only after I moved it and sat beside him. He leaned against her left shoulder. Corven waited until Teyo crooked two fingers at him. Then he joined them, plain and careful, and offered his hand instead of taking Teyo's.

Pippa pulled me into the hall while Teyo ate toast with honey. “Now they can ask the godparent thing,” she said. “But not because I fed him. He would've got fed anyway.”

“Agreed.”

“And I talk first if it's for me.”

“You ask first. We decide together.”

Back in the flight room, Corven wiped honey from his sleeve while Teyo denied putting it there. The power remained out, but his temperature had begun to rise.

“Explain the offer,” I said. “Exact obligations. No ceremony.”

Corven straightened. “Godparent is the nearest English term, not an exact translation. In our family, adults may make one optional pledge to a household whose child has sheltered theirs. Until Pippa turns sixteen, we would owe her truthful warning of any danger our family causes or brings near her, as much as three nights of emergency shelter, and practical help such as transport, food, or supplies when we can provide it safely.”

“What do you get?” Pippa asked.

“No custody,” he said. “No access to you or your home. No obedience, secrecy, service, or claim. We do not become family unless you use that word. Refusing causes no offense.”

Olya said, “And this is our gratitude to carry. Not yours. Not Teyo's.”

“Can you ask again if I say no?”

“No,” Corven said. “Not unless you invite the question.”

“Why me?”

Olya started with a sentence, lost it, and touched the damp patch over her own knee. “Because you kept noticing what he did. Because when we were foolish at the door, you—”

“I told you about the board,” Pippa said. “That doesn't mean you know me.”

“No.” Olya gave a small nod. “It is what I know tonight. The pledge can stay unmade.”

Pippa and I went to the kitchen alone. She asked whether emergency shelter meant sleeping in the wing coat. I said we could prohibit the coat. She asked if they could take her anywhere. I said not under the offer and not under any agreement I would accept. She asked whether Teyo got to be her friend without the adults' pledge.

“Yes,” I said. “Separately. With the usual rules.”

“Group messages?”

“No hidden messages. No deleting. At first, the family account.”

“That's annoying.”

“It is.”

She ate half a piece of Teyo's toast while she thought. Rainwater crawled down the dark kitchen windows. At last she said, “One year. Then we both have to say yes again. You and me.”

“Either of us can end it sooner.”

“And no surprise visits. They knocked like a horror film.”

“No unsupervised visits or outings.”

“Not even flying ones,” she said, and that decided it.
